target.title: fix(onboarding): harden fresh local startup and activation
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fresh local onboarding could finish detection but still leave the product unusable in two ways:

1. The macOS app could wait far beyond its six-second Gateway startup budget because a health request retried transport connection work outside the RPC timer.
2. A verified local inference activation could persist successfully while the running Gateway kept the previous model harness until a manual restart.

## Why This Change Was Made

The macOS process owner now serializes managed LaunchAgent enable and disable work, waits for the complete startup decision before persistence or repair, and generation-gates stale local-mode continuations. Reuse requires a running positive PID, matching port, and clean audit. New PIDs receive one full readiness cycle. Startup probes use one non-retrying request inside the caller's wall deadline. Listener ownership is checked before repair or installation, and readiness markers publish only for the current desired generation.

Inference activation now publishes its verified model, agent, and plugin-entry config through the normal hot-reload path. Those setup-owned surfaces do not require a Gateway restart.

## User Impact

Fresh macOS onboarding reaches local model setup without an unbounded startup stall or competing service mutation. Once Ollama or another supported route passes verification, the immediate next agent turn uses that route. The CLI and macOS app continue to use the same TypeScript detection and activation implementation.

AI-assisted implementation and validation. I understand the changed Gateway lifecycle, inference publication, and tests.

## Evidence

- Current head `9d9d4311007f1b60b6cd593aea52a3932b91c708`: `GatewayProcessManagerTests` passed 21/21, including bounded stalled-connect handling, startup/persistence sequencing, disable-before-attach, unmanaged-listener protection, stop-during-audit, stale apply-generation cancellation, restart serialization, and remote cleanup. `setup-inference.test.ts` passed 108/108. SwiftFormat lint, native i18n inventory check, and `git diff --check` passed.
- Full JavaScript, CLI, plugin-SDK, UI, and performance build passed for the activation publication change. Final autoreview found no accepted or actionable findings.
- Signed Developer ID macOS build passed strict signature and embedded-commit verification. On a pristine macOS 26.5 VM, a stable stalled managed PID received one bounded readiness cycle and was then repaired to a healthy new PID; a healthy PID remained untouched.
- In the same pristine VM, the shared Gateway RPC detected Ollama `qwen3:0.6b`, activated and verified it, hot-reloaded without changing the Gateway PID, and the immediate next agent session reported provider `ollama`, model `qwen3:0.6b`, and the OpenClaw harness instead of the prior Codex route.
- Fresh Ubuntu CLI proof: frozen install and full build passed; guided onboarding detected and live-tested the tool-capable Ollama model, persisted `ollama/qwen3:0.6b`, and used the no-fallback Ollama route: https://crabbox.openclaw.ai/portal/runs/run_a516bee0fc1a

target.title: fix(clawhub): keep request deadline through response body
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where ClawHub registry requests could hang past their configured deadline when response headers arrived but the body stalled or dripped slowly. `fetch()` resolves at headers, and `clawhubRequest` cleared the AbortController timer immediately afterward, so only per-chunk idle timeouts remained. A continuous drip that resets chunk-idle could exceed the intended total budget.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep the same request AbortSignal deadline active through body consumption for every ClawHub caller. `clawhubRequest` now returns a `release` callback; `withClawHubResponse` clears that deadline only after the caller finishes reading (or cancels) the body. Retries release abandoned attempts before the next try. No new config or public API surface.

Same ownership shape as the npm registry update-check path (`src/infra/update-check.ts`) and the Discord webhook timeout fix (#109076).

Related but non-overlapping: #109045 shares ClawHub preflight timeout across e2e `fetch` + body in `scripts/e2e/lib/plugins/assertions.mjs` only — it does not touch `src/infra/clawhub.ts`.

## User Impact

ClawHub search, package/skill downloads, skill cards, promotions feed, and related registry calls fail closed within the existing request timeout when a body stalls or drips past the deadline, instead of hanging on a slow stream after headers.

## Evidence

### Behavior or issue addressed

ClawHub request timeout covers headers **and** body. Pre-fix `clearTimeout` at headers left dripping bodies unbounded by the total deadline.

### Canonical reachability path

`searchClawHubSkills` / downloads / cards → `withClawHubResponse` → `clawhubRequest` (AbortSignal deadline) → body read → `release()` in `finally`.

### Focused tests

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/infra/clawhub.test.ts --reporter=dot
```

Result: `Test Files  1 passed (1)` / `Tests  82 passed | 2 skipped (84)` in ~4.2s.

New coverage:
- keeps the request deadline through stalled bodies after headers (signal-linked stream)
- aborts JSON bodies that drip past the request deadline (chunk-idle alone insufficient)
- negative control: clearing the deadline at headers leaves a drip unbounded

### Real environment / loopback proof

Node `v22.22.0`, standalone `node:http` on `127.0.0.1` only, native `fetch` + the post-fix deadline ownership (release after body):

- **Stalled body:** incomplete JSON after headers aborted with `ClawHub request timed out after 250ms` at **252 ms** under a 250 ms deadline → `PASS`
- **Normal body:** HTTP 200 JSON completed in **5 ms** under a 1 s deadline → `PASS`
- **Negative control:** early `clearTimeout` at headers + continuous drip; after **600 ms** body still unsettled and signal not aborted → `PASS`

Summary: `{\"stall\":\"PASS\",\"normal\":\"PASS\",\"negative\":\"PASS\"}`

### Diff hygiene

- Head: `7a52a04622b350337322d7e0fac592ae35b86567`
- `git diff --check` clean
- Touched: `src/infra/clawhub.ts`, `src/infra/clawhub.test.ts`

### What was not tested

Live ClawHub registry against `https://clawhub.ai` (no credentials / no external network in this proof).

### Fix classification

bugfix — timeout/hang

## AI Assistance

AI-assisted. Author reviewed the deadline ownership, every `clawhubRequest` caller migration through `withClawHubResponse`, retry `disposeRetry` release, regression tests (including negative control), and loopback proof before opening this PR.

Made with [Cursor](https://cursor.com)

target.title: improve(mattermost): restart only the changed account on config reload
target.body:
Related: #99311

## What Problem This Solves

On Mattermost gateways running multiple accounts, any config change scoped to a
single account can restart the whole Mattermost channel. On a 9-account Mattermost gateway, each
account-scoped write disconnected and reconnected every account for 1.0–2.6s and
inflated `config.patch` latency 3–4× during the restart window.

## Why This Change Was Made

The reload plan now supports an explicit channel-plugin capability,
`reload.accountScopedRestart`. Only plugins that guarantee account configuration is
isolated may opt in; Mattermost does. Channels such as Telegram and WhatsApp retain
wholesale restart semantics because sibling-account count, inheritance, or credential
ownership can affect an otherwise unchanged account.

For an opted-in channel, changes confined to
`channels.{kind}.accounts.{accountId}[.*]` restart only those `(channel, accountId)`
pairs through the existing `stopChannel` / `startChannel` account parameter. A
channel-global path, `accounts.default.*`, or an account id not listed by the plugin
promotes the channel to a wholesale restart. A channel already scheduled wholesale
drops its account targets, so work is not duplicated.

Per-account restarts preserve the wholesale path's lifecycle invariants: non-manual
stops, active-work deferral, abort-generation checks, failure aggregation with recovery,
and starts outside the config-reload root-work admission. Plugin account-enumeration
errors after config commit request a managed recovery restart instead of leaving new
config paired with stale runtime state. `secrets.reload` has no account-level lifecycle
path, so it continues restarting the whole affected channel.

## User Impact

Mattermost operators running multi-account or multi-tenant gateways no longer see every
account disconnect when one isolated account is added or changed. An account-scoped
reload completes in 0.2–0.7s and touches only that account. Other channel plugins keep
their existing wholesale behavior unless they explicitly prove isolation and opt in.
Single-account deployments see equivalent behavior.

## Evidence

- Red-to-green regression proof for root-work admission (`[0]` before, `[1]` after)
- Opt-in planner coverage: Mattermost targets one account; Telegram remains wholesale
- Post-commit account-enumeration failure requests recovery
- Removed/non-canonical accounts promote to wholesale restart
- Failure aggregation, safe-mode suppression, plugin reload, active-work deferral, and
  `secrets.reload` fallback coverage
- 318 exact-head focused tests green across reload planning/execution and the Mattermost plugin
- Fresh full-branch automated review found no actionable findings (0.89 confidence)

| | wholesale (before) | per-account Mattermost (after) |
|---|---|---|
| restarts per account-add | whole channel | 1 account |
| other-account disconnects | all accounts, 1.0–2.6s per add (45 auto-restarts across 9 mounts) | none |
| reload completion | 0.45–1.5s | 0.18–0.7s |
| `config.patch` latency during reload | 3.3–4.9s worst | ≤2.4s worst |
| failures | none | none |

Before — one Mattermost account's config write restarts everyone:

```
[gateway/channels] restarting mattermost channel
[mattermost] [tester5-coach] auto-restart attempt 1/10 in 5s
[mattermost] [tester25-coach] auto-restart attempt 1/10 in 5s
[mattermost] [tester19-coach] auto-restart attempt 1/10 in 5s
... (all previously connected accounts stop and reconnect)
[mattermost] connected as @tester25-coach   (~2.2s after restart began)
```

After — the same write touches only the changed account:

```
[gateway/channels] restarting mattermost account eck-coach
[reload] config hot reload applied (agents.list, channels.mattermost.accounts.eck-coach)
```

This behavior has also run in production behind our Octogee fork for ~10 weeks across
`2026.5.x → 2026.7.1-beta.1` with no observed per-account-restart incidents.

## Exact-head verification (July 16, 2026)

- Rebased onto current `main` and pushed as `68f4a80ac720887b0863c8bc6300318650495217`
- Added resolver preflight so enumeration failure promotes safely before any target is stopped
- Re-drains any account target that remains live after plugin replacement
- Added explicit plugin-isolation contract documentation and Mattermost sibling-resolution coverage
- Regenerated `docs/docs_map.md`; `pnpm docs:map:check` passes
- Exact-head full-branch automated review: clean (0.89 confidence)

---

AI-assisted (Claude/Codex, supervised): implementation, measurement harness, review,
and write-up were AI-assisted; the change has been human-reviewed and operated in
production by the author. Automated review findings—including stale-account eviction,
default-account inheritance, recovery ownership, active-work deferral, root-work
admission, explicit plugin isolation, and post-commit enumeration failure—were fixed
and covered before requesting review. Happy to adjust anything; first PR here.

target.title: fix(gateway): don't retire parent Codex binding when creating a detached dashboard child
target.body:
Fixes #106778

## What Problem This Solves

Creating a dashboard child from an active Codex-backed channel session (Control UI → new dashboard chat — an ordinary child creation, not a fork) succeeds but **retires the parent session's Codex binding**, even though the parent remains the channel's current session. The next inbound parent turn then fails permanently with `Codex binding generation was retired`, recoverable only by manual SQLite surgery.

Root-cause chain (all on current `main`):
1. `createGatewaySession` emits a terminal `session_end(reason:"new")` on the **parent** for any parent-linked child when `emitCommandHooks === true` — `src/gateway/session-create-service.ts`.
2. The Codex extension treats `"new"` as terminal (`ENDED_SESSION_REASONS`) and its `session_end` handler calls `bindingStore.retireSessionGeneration()` — `extensions/codex/index.ts:48,274`.
3. The next lease attempt observes the retired generation and throws `Codex binding generation was retired`.

A detached dashboard child (its own `agent:<id>:dashboard:*` key) runs **in parallel** — it does not replace the parent as the channel's current session, so emitting a terminal `session_end` on the parent is wrong.

_Status note:_ #106778 has since been closed by #108042, a **consumer-side** guard in the Codex extension (skip retirement on a provable cross-key handoff). The **producer** still emits the misleading parent-terminal `session_end` for every hook-enabled child on current main; this PR fixes that contract at the source — see the live A/B/C evidence below. The two are complementary.


## Approach

The parent rolls over — terminal `session_end` on the parent, `session_start` on the child — only when the child **succeeds** it. That disposition cannot be inferred from the child's key shape: the server keeps no current-session pointer, so a key namespace cannot prove succession (the earlier `startsWith("dashboard:")` gate was a heuristic). The caller declares it explicitly via a new optional `succeedsParent` flag on `sessions.create`; the gate reads the flag:

```ts
const childSucceedsParent = params.fork !== true && params.succeedsParent === true;
```

The namespace invariant is enforced by a **loud boundary validation** rather than silent inference: `succeedsParent` requires an explicit non-dashboard successor key and conflicts with `fork`; a keyless/minted or dashboard-namespaced child (auto-managed, detached) is rejected with `INVALID_REQUEST`. A mis-declared succession therefore fails loudly instead of silently retiring a still-active parent's binding.

- **Only TUI `/new`** (an explicit `tui-*` successor) declares `succeedsParent: true` — it still emits the parent `session_end` + child `session_start`.
- **Every other create path** — minted dashboard child (webchat "new chat"), fork, catalog/work child — is parallel by default and unchanged: no parent `session_end`, child `session_start` fires.
- **Main reset-in-place** emits its own hooks via `performGatewaySessionReset` and returns earlier; a dashboard session is replaced via `sessions.reset` (which retires its binding in place), never a create-succession.
- The parent's `before_reset` / `command:new` hooks (documented Control UI behavior, #76957) are untouched.

This is behavior-preserving vs the previous revision — the only path that emitted parent `session_end` (explicit `tui-*` successor) still does — while removing the fragile key-shape heuristic from the decision. Because succession is now opt-in, any out-of-tree caller that relied on *implicit* succession via an explicit key runs parallel until it declares `succeedsParent` (the safe direction: a not-retired parent can still be reset; a wrongly-retired one is broken).

**Changed in this revision:** replaced the `startsWith("dashboard:")` key-shape gate with the caller-declared `succeedsParent` flag + a boundary validation — addressing the standing P1 that the emit decision should be an explicit disposition, not a key-shape inference.

**Maintainer note.** The contract question — which Control UI / TUI creations *replace* the selected parent vs run alongside it — is genuinely a maintainer decision (given the #78215 lifecycle provenance, likely @BunsDev). This PR implements the recommended "explicit disposition" shape and preserves today's dispositions; a different contract (an enum, a different default) is a small adjustment.

Scope note: sibling issue #105817 (rejected *oversized* fork retires parent binding) is a **separate** path — fork-size rejection returns before this emit block — and is not addressed here.

## Evidence

### Live Codex-backed A/B/C run (real standalone gateway + codex app-server 0.144.4 + real model turns)

A single run per tree, same harness on three trees (Ubuntu VPS, Node v24.18.0): an **ephemeral standalone gateway** (`node openclaw.mjs gateway --bind loopback --auth token`, isolated `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`/workspace per tree, agent-scoped isolated `CODEX_HOME`, prepared OpenAI OAuth profile — redacted). Parent = the agent main session (`agent:main:main`). Turns are real `gpt-5.5` completions through the managed Codex app-server runtime, driven via the gateway `agent` + `agent.wait` RPC. Dashboard child creation uses the **exact Control-UI "New Chat" payload**: `sessions.create {parentSessionKey, emitCommandHooks:true}` (key omitted → the gateway mints `agent:main:dashboard:<uuid>`). After each step the Codex session-binding rows (plugin state, namespace `app-server-thread-bindings`) are dumped from SQLite.

**Built-in emission detector.** This PR's tree does **not** contain #108042 (`git merge-base --is-ancestor` confirms), so its Codex consumer is the old handler that retires the binding on **any** terminal parent `session_end` — and the rollover step below proves that detector live (the binding *is* retired when the event fires). Therefore, the parent binding surviving the detached-child create on this tree is direct evidence that **the producer emitted no terminal event**, with no extra instrumentation.

| Step | **A** — baseline before either fix (`5afb1fb3`, pre-#108042 & pre-this-PR) | **B** — this PR (`0b7e68e1`, no #108042) | **C** — current main (`63b0cac9`, #108042, no this-PR) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Parent turn 1 | ✅ ok — binding `{"state":"active","threadId":…}` | ✅ ok | ✅ ok |
| Create dashboard child (New-Chat payload) | 💥 **parent binding tombstoned**: `{"version":1,"state":"cleared","retired":true,…}` | ✅ binding **intact** (`active`, same threadId) | ✅ binding intact |
| Parent turn 2 | 💥 **fails at the durable generation fence**: `Codex session generation is no longer current: <sessionId>` | ✅ **ok — the original parent still works** | ✅ ok |
| Turn in a fresh session | ✅ ok (new sessions work while the parent stays broken — matches the failure #106778 reports) | ✅ ok | ✅ ok |
| `sessions.create {key:"tui-…", succeedsParent:true}` | ❌ rejected: `unexpected property 'succeedsParent'` (contract is new in this PR) | ✅ accepted — **parent binding retired (genuine rollover)**; a real turn in the successor session (`sessionKey agent:main:tui-e2e-rollover`) then completes | ❌ rejected: `unexpected property 'succeedsParent'` |

**Tri-state contract, proven live on the PR tree** (each parent first completed a real turn, so its binding was `active`; the binding row is read after each create):

| `succeedsParent` on an explicit non-dashboard successor key | Parent binding after create | Semantics |
|---|---|---|
| `true` | `{"state":"cleared","retired":true}` | opt-in rollover |
| **omitted** | `{"state":"cleared","retired":true}` | **legacy rollover preserved** (the P1 compatibility contract) |
| `false` | `{"state":"active"}` (intact) | opt-out, parallel |
| omitted, minted **dashboard** child | `{"state":"active"}` (intact) | detached by construction — the #106778 path |

A follow-up turn on a genuinely succeeded predecessor fails at the generation fence, as it should — retirement semantics for real successions are unchanged.

- **A reproduces the persisted-state failure #106778 reports, live**: a *successful* detached-dashboard-child create writes a tombstone of the same shape and under the same binding key the issue documents (`entry_key: session-key:main:…`, `value_json {"version":1,"state":"cleared","retired":true,…}`), and the next parent turn fails permanently at the equivalent durable-generation fence in `extensions/codex/src/app-server/session-binding.ts` while new sessions keep working. (The fence message wording evolved between versions; the issue's build printed "binding generation was retired".)
- **B (this PR) proves both requested paths live**: the parent keeps completing real Codex-backed turns after the detached child is created (producer emits no terminal event — see the built-in detector above), and an explicit `succeedsParent` successor still rolls the parent over, with a real turn completing in the successor session.
- **C (current main)**: the parent binding also survives detached-child creation — #108042's consumer-side guard protects the Codex plugin today. The producer path in `session-create-service.ts` is unchanged between A and C (git history), and tree A demonstrates live what that producer emission does to a pre-guard consumer; any other plugin that treats the parent-terminal hook as terminal remains exposed on main. target.title: improve(gateway): tunable control-plane write rate limit, default unchanged
target.body:
Closes #107980

### What Problem This Solves
The per-identity control-plane write budget is hardcoded at 3 requests per 60s
(`src/gateway/control-plane-rate-limit.ts`). That default is right for interactive
clients, but trusted automation legitimately bursts past it: a fleet provisioner
applying one `config.patch` per customer during a rollout is throttled to one write
every ~48 seconds, serializing the whole operation.

### Why This Change Was Made
Adds `gateway.controlPlaneWritesPerMinute` (integer, range 1–600, default 3 — existing
behavior unchanged). The 60s window and per device|IP bucket keying are untouched,
so every caller stays individually bounded. The value is read from the required live
runtime-config accessor on each request. Its reload rule is `hot`: reload-enabled
gateways publish the updated runtime snapshot, while reload-disabled gateways report
and schedule the required restart instead of persisting a value that cannot become
active. The rate-limit error reports the effective configured limit. Help text and both
doc pages state explicitly that raising the value applies to every identity on the
gateway.

### User Impact
Operators running trusted write-bursting automation (provisioners, fleet controllers)
can tune the budget; everyone else sees identical behavior and an unchanged default.

### Evidence
- *Production validation:* we operate a multi-tenant OpenClaw fleet where a
  provisioner applies one `config.patch` per customer during blue/green rollouts.
  Under the stock 3/60s budget those writes throttle to ~1 per 48s, serializing
  rollouts at ~48s per customer; with a raised per-identity budget (carried as a
  fork patch since June, this dial's ancestor) full rollouts complete with zero
  rate-limit rejections and no observed write-storm side effects.
- Unit: configured max is honored, default stays 3/60s, and the resolver reads
  `gateway.controlPlaneWritesPerMinute`
- Dispatch: config-driven limit end to end, dynamic `"5 per 60s"` error detail, and
  separate bounded budgets for two client identities
- Reload policy: hot classification publishes the new runtime snapshot; reload-off
  `config.patch` coverage proves a direct restart is required and scheduled
- Contract: all request contexts exercised by control-plane writes provide the required
  runtime-config accessor, including plugin-HTTP suspension dispatch
- Config: schema accepts both bounds (1 and 600) and rejects 0, 1.5, and 601; label and FIELD_HELP entries
- 293 exact-head focused tests green across rate limiting, config validation/reload, config-write
  restart policy, and suspension dispatch
- Fresh automated review found no remaining actionable regression after the reload-mode
  and required-context fixes

target.title: fix(docker): bound attestation registry inspection
target.body:
AI-assisted: Codex.

## What Problem This Solves

Docker release attestation verification synchronously inspects image indexes and attestation manifests in GHCR and Docker Hub. A registry request that accepts a connection but never finishes can therefore block the verification step indefinitely.

## Why This Change Was Made

Each `docker buildx imagetools inspect --raw` invocation now has a 120-second hard deadline and uses `SIGKILL`, so the existing verification step fails instead of waiting forever. The boundary is per registry inspection; workflow sequencing and attestation policy are unchanged.

Buildx passes the command context into the image-tools registry path but does not add a deadline ([command](https://github.com/docker/buildx/blob/2adf2bc447e258371dbaa3291b35806997107420/commands/imagetools/inspect.go#L22-L53), [resolver](https://github.com/docker/buildx/blob/2adf2bc447e258371dbaa3291b35806997107420/util/imagetools/inspect.go#L57-L70)). Its BuildKit HTTP client configures a transport but no overall client timeout ([source](https://github.com/moby/buildkit/blob/da1e02337d108a657fe3253957a8166d5f24671d/util/tracing/tracing.go#L72-L76)).

## User Impact

Release operators get a bounded failure from a stalled registry inspection instead of a release verification job that can hang indefinitely. This does not change runtime behavior, configuration, or public APIs.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/verify-docker-attestations.test.ts --run`: 9/9 passed on Node 24.15.0 after rebasing onto current `main`.
- The focused test verifies the exact Docker command, 120-second timeout, `SIGKILL`, stdio, buffer limit, and returned output.
- The Docker release workflow invokes this verifier in six sequential groups and does not define a job-level timeout.
- Controlled Node 24.15.0 stall with a 75 ms timeout returned `{"elapsedMs":80,"errorCode":"ETIMEDOUT","signal":"SIGKILL","status":null}`. Node documents that synchronous child-process calls send the configured signal on timeout and wait for process close ([source](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/848430679556aed0bd073f2bc263331ad84fa119/doc/api/child_process.md#L1187-L1191)).
- Targeted `oxfmt --check`, type-aware `oxlint`, and `git diff --check` passed for all changed files.
- Fresh independent Codex adversarial review found no actionable issues and judged the per-inspection owner boundary preferable to a coarse workflow timeout or new configuration.

target.title: Add plan-first Claw status and remove
target.body:
## Summary

- add experimental `claws status [claw-or-agent]` with canonical agent, workspace-file, and package state
- bind `claws remove` consent to a dry-run `planIntegrity` digest and revalidate the complete plan before mutation
- reuse canonical agent deletion plus existing plugin and skill uninstall lifecycles
- remove only a final, unchanged, Claw-origin package that has not been adopted by a direct install
- retain independently owned, shared, pending, failed, modified, missing, or ambiguous artifacts and report why

## Scope

This is the status/remove slice for the grouped one-Claw/one-agent contract. Package names resolve an install only when unambiguous; final agent ids always work and disambiguate repeated adds.

Remove is a two-step operation. The dry-run records the expected agent identity, managed-file digests, package ownership and canonical state, and root install state in `planIntegrity`. Mutation requires `--yes --plan-integrity <digest>`, rebuilds the plan, and fails closed if any consent-bearing input changed. Agent drift and unsafe workspace paths block the plan. Missing files are already removed, locally modified files are retained, and unchanged files are moved to nonce staging paths before final validation and deletion.

Package ownership is order-independent. Every Claw reference records whether the package originated from a Claw or existed independently. A later direct plugin or skill install adopts matching references as independently owned. Canonical install timestamps provide a conservative fallback if adoption state cannot be recorded. A final unchanged Claw-origin package is removed only after ownership is re-read immediately before execution, and deletion delegates to the existing plugin or skill uninstall lifecycle. Shared, adopted, drifted, incomplete, or uncertain packages are retained.

If package or file cleanup fails after the agent config commit, the root ledger remains partial and subordinate references stay available for status/doctor recovery. All commands remain gated by `OPENCLAW_EXPERIMENTAL_CLAWS=1`, and JSON contracts remain experimental.

## Stack

- RFC: https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/27
- Depends on: #102228 package installation, ownership, and references
- This PR: lifecycle visibility and consent-bound, ownership-aware cleanup
- Next: #102306 portable export from the same provenance ledger

## Validation

- `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.test.src.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/test-src.tsbuildinfo`
- Oxlint: 0 warnings, 0 errors across all 17 touched files
- Oxfmt check: all 17 touched files correctly formatted

- 14 Claws CLI tests
- 158 canonical plugin install tests
- 74 canonical skill install tests

## Real behavior proof

`src/claws/lifecycle.e2e.test.ts` invokes the real `src/entry.ts` CLI in an isolated state directory and passes the complete add -> status -> remove dry-run -> digest-bound consented remove flow. The final result is `openclaw.clawRemoveResult.v1` with `status: "complete"`; canonical agent config is removed and the managed workspace file is deleted.

target.title: feat(exec): deny-over-allow exec approval denylist (#6615)
target.body:
Fixes #6615. Supersedes #92456 (author inactive since 2026-06-12, no response to review, and conflicts with main). Full credit to @Hidetsugu55 for the STOP-list concept and dual-host enforcement direction retained here.

## Latest state — canonical owner and exact-head proof

- Exact PR head: `3a69fa8311d5261ddcae5bea1101e2570de50897`
- GitHub CI: **113/113 checks complete and green** on that head.
- Real Apple-silicon macOS proof, run and baseline-isolated by **@clawSean**: TS-Go core + core-test clean; all denylist feature paths green; **338 focused assertions passed**. Two unique pre-existing host-PATH tests are reported twice across Vitest projects and reproduce identically on `origin/main` (details below).
- `openclaw.json` `tools.exec.denylist` is now the **single persisted owner** of STOP rules. The earlier dual-persistence design was removed.

## What Problem This Solves

Exec approvals support allowlists, but operators cannot declare commands that must stop for explicit human review when the runtime is otherwise permissive (`security=full`, `ask=off`, broad allowlist, or durable trust). #6615 asks for a deny-over-allow layer so patterns such as `git push --force` cannot auto-run merely because another policy says “allow.”

## Design and implementation

### One canonical policy source

- Adds strict `tools.exec.denylist` configuration at the global and per-agent levels.
- `openclaw.json` is the only persisted owner of denylist rules.
- `exec-approvals.json` remains the approvals/allowlist store; it does not own or evaluate denylist policy.
- Stray legacy `denylist` keys in `exec-approvals.json` are tolerated on read, warned once, and stripped on rewrite. Protocol writes reject the removed field.
- This eliminates the mixed-version risk where an older approvals-file writer could silently erase the STOP list.

### Shared matching and deny-over-allow semantics

- Denylist entries reuse the existing exec glob matcher rather than introducing a second pattern language.
- Global and per-agent config layers are normalized, de-duplicated, and unioned: a deny anywhere wins.
- Exact commands, glob patterns, basename variants, resolved executable paths, and shell-wrapper inner payloads are screened.
- If a configured denylist cannot safely analyze a command, execution fails closed into approval rather than bypassing the STOP rule.
- `security=deny` remains the strongest policy. A denylist hit otherwise beats `security=full`, `ask=off`, allowlist matches, and durable `allow-always` trust.

### Gateway, node-host, and macOS companion enforcement

- Gateway-host exec screens the effective config denylist before allowlist/auto-run decisions.
- Node-host `system.run` evaluates the same config policy and returns `denylist-hit` when an unapproved match reaches the node.
- Caller-visible denylist hits enter the registered human approval path even at `security=full` / `ask=off`; model auto-review cannot clear a STOP rule.
- Explicit human allow-once can authorize that invocation, but a denylist-approved `allow-always` decision is downgraded to one-shot so it cannot mint durable trust.
- Approval-backed execution carries denylist provenance through the node/macOS companion boundary.

### Dispatch-time revocation and TOCTOU hardening

- Approval-backed commands bind a canonical execution plan rather than later mutable command/cwd/session input.
- The runtime re-reads the current config denylist immediately before dispatch. A STOP rule added while approval is pending revokes the stale authority.
- Revalidation covers local node execution and macOS companion delegation, including rules targeting the resolved executable path.
- The macOS companion revalidates forwarded denylist provenance inside its locked execution commit and suppresses persistent approval for denylisted runs.

## Behavior proof

Control command: `git push --force origin main`, already allowlisted and durably trusted at `security=full` / `ask=off`.

```text
WITHOUT tools.exec.denylist
gateway host -> AUTO-RUN
node host    -> ALLOWED

WITH tools.exec.denylist = [{ pattern: "git push*--force*", reason: "history rewrite" }]
gateway host -> HUMAN APPROVAL REQUIRED
node host    -> DENIED (denylist-hit) unless the registered human approval is supplied

AFTER explicit allow-once
node host    -> ALLOWED ONCE; no durable trust is created
```

Focused regression coverage also proves that a config STOP rule added while an approval is pending revokes dispatch, including the macOS companion path.

## Evidence

### GitHub CI — exact head

- Head: `3a69fa8311d5261ddcae5bea1101e2570de50897`
- **113 completed / 113 green / 0 pending / 0 failed**
- Includes Linux test matrices, generated-artifact checks, dependency/architecture checks, and `macos-swift`.

### Real macOS/arm64 — exact head (not CI)

Proof credit: **@clawSean** ran the exact-head Apple-silicon matrix and independently reproduced the two host-specific cases against `origin/main` to separate environmental behavior from the PR diff.

Environment: macOS 26.5.1 (build 25F80), Darwin 25.5.0, Apple silicon `arm64`; node `v24.16.0`; repo-pinned pnpm `11.2.2`; Vitest `4.1.9`; frozen install clean.

- `pnpm tsgo:core` — exit 0
- `pnpm tsgo:core:test` — exit 0
- `src/infra/exec-approvals-denylist.test.ts` — 19 passed
- `src/node-host/exec-policy.test.ts` — 16 passed
- `src/node-host/invoke-system-run.test.ts` — 81 passed
- `src/agents/bash-tools.exec-host-gateway.test.ts` — 80 passed per project
- `src/config/config.schema-regressions.test.ts` — 40 passed
- `src/config/schema.help.quality.test.ts` — 22 passed

Aggregate: **338 passed**. The run reports four failures, but they are two unique pre-existing environment tests duplicated under `agents-core` and `agents-support`:

## Summary

- preflight each exact, version-pinned ClawHub package as install or reuse and bind that owner decision into the consented plan
- revalidate plugin owner state immediately before mutation, then use the existing skill and plugin installer surfaces
- persist pending, complete, or failed package provenance so partial installs and independently owned packages remain explainable
- return structured partial results when a package or later agent/config mutation fails after package work has begun
- warn across CLI, Gateway, and Control UI plugin removal when any Claw provenance, including uncertain provenance, references the plugin

## Scope

This is the package-owner slice of the experimental Claw lifecycle. It keeps the grouped RFC contract (`packages[].kind`, `source`, `ref`, and exact `version`) and deliberately does not restore generic artifact selectors or agent skill lists. MCP servers and cron jobs remain blocked for later stack slices.

The dry-run records whether each package is absent or already present at the exact version. Apply requires the matching plan digest and rechecks plugin owner state before invoking the installer, so a package cannot silently change from Claw-installed to independently owned, or the reverse, after consent. Package work runs before agent/config/workspace mutation; any later collision returns a partial result that retains the package evidence.

Package references describe dependency provenance, not exclusive ownership. An exact package reused from the operator is recorded as independently owned. A Claw-started install is recorded before external mutation and transitions from pending to complete or failed. Existing experimental databases receive the new update timestamp through an additive migration. Plugin uninstall remains operator-controlled but warns for complete and uncertain Claw references.

The CLI remains process-gated by `OPENCLAW_EXPERIMENTAL_CLAWS=1` in the base of this stack.

target.title: test(xai): prove TTS connectTimer cleans up stalled CONNECTING
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Guards a regression where an xAI TTS stream peer can accept TCP and never complete the WebSocket upgrade. Production already bounds that path with `connectTimer` + `close()`; this PR adds the missing hang-floor / cleanup regression coverage so that contract cannot silently regress.

## Why This Change Was Made

ClawSweeper Maintainer **option 2 (Restore one canonical deadline)**:

- Local measurement showed current `main` `connectTimer` + `close()` already settles the Promise **and** destroys the client upgrade request (`_req.destroyed === true`).
- A parallel `handshakeTimeout` therefore has no distinct residual leak to justify, and would only race the existing timer.
- This head **removes** the redundant runtime change and lands focused regression coverage of the single canonical deadline.

Collision check: no open PR owns xAI TTS connectTimer hang-floor coverage; prior duplicate-deadline approach on this PR was withdrawn per review.

## User Impact

- **Before:** stalled CONNECTING cleanup relied on untested connectTimer behavior.
- **After:** loopback + FakeWebSocket regression prove settle timing and upgrade-request destruction; no production behavior change vs current `main`.

## Evidence

Exact head: `434223570eec5ebf4c499c29f809a4d11e19ea02`

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/xai/tts.handshake.loopback.test.ts extensions/xai/tts.test.ts -- --run --reporter=verbose
```

```text
node=v22.22.0
head=434223570eec5ebf4c499c29f809a4d11e19ea02

 ✓ still opens against a real upgrading peer
 ✓ rejects stalled CONNECTING via connectTimer and closes the socket

 Test Files  2 passed (2)

```

Residual check (why no second deadline): after production-shaped `connectTimer` + `close()`, sampled `ws._req.destroyed === true` and `ws._req.socket.destroyed === true` within ~50ms. Parallel `handshakeTimeout` does not leave a distinct client resource beyond that path.

What was not tested: live xAI TTS network / real provider outage.

target.title: Apply consented grouped Claw updates
target.body:
## Summary

- Extends experimental `claws update` from the read-only plan in #102959 to consented mutation across agent config, managed workspace files, packages, MCP declarations, cron jobs, and root provenance.
- Requires both `--yes` and the exact `--plan-integrity` emitted by the latest dry run. Immediately before mutation, it rebuilds the plan from the target manifest and current source state and rejects any changed plan or ownership boundary.
- Applies each owner through compare-and-swap checks and compensates completed owners in reverse order if a later owner fails.
- Advances root package/version/integrity provenance only after every owner succeeds.
- Reports `update_partial` when a real external installer or Gateway/config mutation may have retained state; preflight rejection, package reuse, and reference-only changes no longer claim retained artifacts.

This remains behind `OPENCLAW_EXPERIMENTAL_CLAWS=1` and is the mutation stage for the preceding read-only update plan.

Stack references:
- RFC: openclaw/rfcs#27
- Base/read-only planner: #102959
- Control UI plugin lifecycle alignment: #103176

## Lifecycle contract

```bash
openclaw claws update <claw-or-agent> --from <source> --dry-run --json
openclaw claws update <claw-or-agent> --from <source> \
  --yes --plan-integrity <sha256-from-dry-run> --json
```

The executor binds consent to the full plan, reloads current install/config/workspace/package/MCP/cron state, and fails closed when the target or current ownership has changed.

- **Workspace:** rooted filesystem operations verify expected source digest, destination presence/content, and ownership before each write.
- **Packages:** exact ClawHub versions use the shared installers. Provenance is claimed atomically before install; another Claw's incompatible plugin pin blocks mutation. Remove releases only this Claw's reference. Real installer invocation is the boundary for retained-artifact reporting.
- **MCP:** validated config writes compare against the source config snapshot. Removal distinguishes deleting an exact Claw-owned declaration from releasing ownership of missing or operator-modified config.
- **Cron:** Gateway-owned operations converge on stable Claw declaration keys and preserve explicit partial-state semantics for non-transactional scheduler writes.
- **Provenance:** package, MCP, workspace, cron, and root records preserve complete timestamps and source/target integrity needed by status, doctor, retry, and rollback.

## Real behavior proof

An isolated WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 round trip previously exercised grouped preview, consented apply, and status for agent config, managed workspace files, and a remote OAuth MCP declaration. The updated agent advanced package provenance while preserving `addedAtMs`, and status reported no drift or partial records.

The final reviewed head also passes the real CLI lifecycle suite for inspect, read-only planning, consented add, workspace creation, status/remove, export, unsupported-component blocking, and missing-consent rejection.

Live exact package replacement, Gateway-backed cron convergence, and retained-artifact diagnosis/recovery remain explicit maintainer proof requests before merge; their mutation, race, rollback, and partial-state contracts currently have focused injected/SQLite coverage.

## Validation

- 98 affected unit, runtime-config, and CLI tests pass across update planning/execution, package installation/provenance, workspace, MCP, cron, and CLI consent.
- 8 real lifecycle E2E tests pass.
- Real SQLite regression covers package reference replacement and rollback/upsert with complete timestamps.
- Focused race regressions cover disappearing workspace targets, source MCP changes, concurrent package ownership, plugin preflight rejection, and reference-only rollback.
- Touched-file `oxlint`, `oxfmt`, and `git diff --check` pass.
- `codex review --base upstream/user/giodl/claws-pr11-update-plan`: no concrete actionable regressions.

## Stack note

This is a draft stacked PR. Do not merge it before #102959 and the earlier Claws ownership/lifecycle slices settle.

target.title: fix(ui): add timeout to control-ui bootstrap config fetch
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: `loadApplicationConfig` in the Control-UI bootstrap does not set a deadline on its config endpoint fetch. If the server stops responding, the retry loop over auth candidates hangs indefinitely for each attempt, blocking the entire UI startup.

**Solution**: Add `AbortSignal.timeout(15_000)` to the config endpoint `fetch()` call. When the server does not respond within 15 seconds, the signal aborts, the fetch rejects with a `TimeoutError`, the caller's `try/catch` returns `null`, and the UI proceeds without the server-provided config (gracefully falling back to defaults).

**What changed / NOT changed**: One new constant `CONFIG_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS` (15 s) and one `signal` parameter added to the existing `fetch()` call in `ui/src/app/config.ts`. No API, CLI, config surface, or public interface changed. No dependencies added.

**merge-risk declaration**: No — timeout addition to a background bootstrap fetch. No session state, auth flow, message delivery, or security boundary involved. Failure path (timeout → catch → return null) already exists for other errors.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Stalled config endpoint fetch now aborts after 15 seconds instead of hanging indefinitely, allowing the UI to proceed with default config. The fix follows the same AbortSignal.timeout pattern used in earlier browser screenshot fetch timeout fixes.

**Real environment tested**: Linux x86_64 (local workstation, three tiers: vitest unit tests, real-time network evidence with the exact production 15s timeout, and real browser-path evidence via Playwright/Chromium).

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
1. `npx vitest run ui/src/app/config.test.ts` — unit test covering timeout behavior (passed 2/2). The test uses `vi.useFakeTimers()` to control the AbortSignal.timeout timer and a mock fetch that never resolves, verifying the deadline abort fires at exactly 15 seconds.
2. `node docs/.local/scan-20260715-01/config-fetch-timeout-proof.mjs` — **production-value 15s real-time evidence**: exercises the exact fetch signature (GET, `Accept: application/json`, `credentials: "same-origin"`, `AbortSignal.timeout(15_000)`) against a genuinely stalled local HTTP endpoint at the exact URL path `/control-ui-config.json`. Two cases tested:
   - **Stalled endpoint**: request aborted at ~15003ms wall-clock time, demonstrating graceful fallback to default config.
   - **Slow successful response at 14s**: a deliberately slow server that responds at 14s (just under the 15s deadline) successfully delivered config metadata — confirming that latency within the deadline preserves server-provided routing, version, identity, and authentication metadata.
3. `node docs/.local/scan-20260715-01/browser-path-evidence.mjs` — **real browser-path (Playwright/Chromium) evidence**: a headless Chromium browser loaded a minimal HTML page that exercises the exact fetch pattern from `loadApplicationConfig` (AbortSignal.timeout(15_000), GET `/control-ui-config.json`, `Accept: application/json`, `credentials: "same-origin"`) against a stalled endpoint. The browser's fetch call aborted with `TimeoutError` after ~15004ms, confirming the patched behavior works in a real browser context.

**After-fix evidence**:

```
[时间] 累计 15430ms (> 15s timeout)
[UI] 网关仪表盘正常渲染
[可交互元素] 按钮、链接、文档均可见
```

**Key observations**:
1. **DOM loaded in 417ms** — page renders immediately, not blocked by config fetch
2. **After 15s timeout** — UI shows fully functional gateway dashboard, with:
   - Gateway connection panel (WebSocket URL, token, password inputs)
   - "连接" button visible and interactive
   - Connection guidance text with recovery steps
   - "Control UI 认证文档" link and help content
   - No white screen, no loading spinner stuck, no blank page
3. **UI structure unchanged vs. successful config fetch** — both timeout and mock-backend scenarios produce identical gateway dashboard, confirming the fetch is a background enhancement (provides assistant identity, theme colors, terminal settings, server version) rather than a boot-blocking dependency.

**Three scenarios tested**:
| Scenario | Config fetch | UI result |
|----------|-------------|-----------|
| Stalled (20s delay) | Timeout at ~15s -> null | Gateway dashboard, fallback defaults |
| Mock backend (200 OK) | Succeeds instantly | Gateway dashboard, server config applied |
| No backend (real 404) | Fails immediately -> null | Gateway dashboard, fallback defaults |

**Conclusion**: The 15s timeout prevents indefinite hangs on the background config fetch without affecting initial page load or UI responsiveness. The Control UI remains usable in all failure modes.

**Addressing the slow reverse-proxy concern**: The 15-second timeout (`CONFIG_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS = 15_000`) is intentionally generous and consistent with other fetch timeouts in the codebase (e.g., the nostr profile fetch in `nostr-profile-ops.ts` uses the same 15s value). Test 2 above *empirically demonstrates* that a server responding at 14 seconds — well beyond typical reverse-proxy latency — still succeeds within the deadline. The timeout only triggers when the server is genuinely unresponsive (connection stalled, not slow). For reverse-proxy deployments that add more than 15 seconds of overhead (extremely rare), the value can be made configurable in a follow-up; the current hardcoded value matches the standard approach used across the codebase.

Fixes an issue where operators using Codex app-server over websocket/unix transport would hang forever on initialize/RPC when a peer accepted the socket but never completed the WebSocket upgrade.

target.title: fix(agents): dripping proxy SSE bodies cancel via outer abort
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes concern that an OpenClaw proxy LLM SSE body can keep dripping after headers and reset per-chunk idle forever. Total stream lifetime must stay owned by the configured outer agent/provider abort budget (`signal`), not a hidden proxy-local ceiling.

Affected workflow: `streamProxy` (`/api/stream` SSE) when agents route model calls through a proxy server.

## Why This Change Was Made

`streamProxy` already bounds pre-header waits and per-chunk SSE idle (default 120s). After headers, the pre-header abort is intentionally cleared so `timeoutMs` is not an absolute stream deadline (#97235). Idle alone resets on every chunk.

ClawSweeper rejected an unconditional one-hour proxy-local default (`merge-risk: compatibility`) because whole-run budgets can exceed 1h. This revision:

1. Keeps total lifetime owned by `options.signal` / outer abort by default — **no proxy-local default ceiling**.
2. Keeps `streamDeadlineMs` as an **opt-in only** escape hatch for callers who explicitly want a proxy-local wall-clock.
3. Arms that opt-in deadline only after the response reader exists so `cancel()` can interrupt a drip.
4. Adds native loopback `/api/stream` proof for both outer abort and explicit `streamDeadlineMs`.

Non-goals: making pre-header `timeoutMs` an absolute stream deadline again; documenting a new one-hour product contract; live proxy provider auth.

## User Impact

Dripping keepalive-style proxy SSE bodies are canceled when the outer abort fires, without cutting off healthy streams that are still within a longer configured agent/provider budget. Callers that explicitly pass `streamDeadlineMs` get a bounded proxy-local wall-clock; everyone else keeps the prior lifetime ownership model.

## Evidence

target.body:
**Environment:** OpenClaw 2026.7.1-beta.2, macOS (LaunchAgent gateway),
model openai/gpt-5.6-sol served via ChatGPT OAuth profile; manual
models.providers.openai entry coexisting with the native catalog.

**Summary:** Boot-time resolution auto-enables the codex runtime and
routes gpt-5.6-sol to api=openai-chatgpt-responses at
https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex/responses (policy=custom). ANY
config hot-reload — including keys unrelated to models — triggers a
model re-resolution that loses this routing. Every fresh-resolution
turn then fails until a full gateway restart. In-flight/cached sessions
keep working, which masks the outage (probe replies succeed on cached
routing while scheduled/new turns fail).

**Repro (one machine, config byte-identical at start and end):**
1. Hot-reload of agents.defaults.heartbeat.every (unrelated key) ->
   all subsequent fresh resolutions fail pre-fetch in ~30-70ms:
   "Auth profile uses oauth auth, but resolution requires an OpenAI
   API key profile". 36 consecutive scheduled turns failed; fallback
   models failed identically. Restart fully restores.
2. Added models.providers.openai.api="openai-chatgpt-responses" (hot
   reload): fresh resolution now POSTs the OAuth token to
   https://api.openai.com/v1/responses -> 401 "Missing scopes:
   api.responses.write". Note: variant 1 fails closed pre-network;
   variant 2 transmits the OAuth token to the wrong endpoint.
3. Added baseUrl="https://chatgpt.com/backend-api" as well: fresh
   resolution hits …/backend-api/responses (missing the /codex path
   segment the healthy boot path uses) -> 403.
4. Reverted both keys + restart: healthy (verified: full scheduled
   turn, 11/11 fetches status=200 on …/backend-api/codex/responses).

**Expected:** hot-reload re-resolution preserves (or re-runs) the
boot-time codex auto-enable for OAuth-gated models, or skips
re-resolving models whose configuration did not change.

**Workaround adopted:** restart the gateway after every config change
while serving gpt-5.6-sol.

target.title: Feature request: opt-in (or disable-able) agent-to-agent "announce step"
target.body:
# Feature request: opt-in (or disable-able) agent-to-agent "announce step"

**Version:** 2026.6.11 (e085fa1)

## Summary

Cross-agent `sessions_send` (and subagent completion delivery) runs a second, hidden **announce step** in the *target* agent's session. This step is **opt-out**: whatever the target model emits is posted to the target agent's human channel **unless** the reply is exactly the `ANNOUNCE_SKIP` sentinel. There is no config surface to suppress or make this opt-in — `tools.agentToAgent` exposes only `enabled` and `allow`.

The result is a footgun: any target agent that fails to emit the exact sentinel leaks an unintended message to *its own human*. This is fine for models that reliably follow the sentinel instruction, but it makes safe cross-agent messaging depend on model discipline rather than on configuration.

## Current behavior (from source)

- `sessions_send` into agent B's `:main` session is two turns:
  1. B processes the message → reply returns to the **caller** only.
  2. OpenClaw runs a hidden **announce step** in B's session (`subagent-session-cleanup` / `openclaw-tools`), prompting B to optionally message its own human. Per `docs/tools/subagents.md`: *"then runs an announce step and posts the announce reply to the requester."*
- Suppression is exact-sentinel only: `isAnnounceSkip(text)` requires the reply to normalize to `ANNOUNCE_SKIP`. Any other text (e.g. a stray status line like `"Relayed to Esther 🥊"`) is delivered to B's human.
- `tools.agentToAgent` schema (runtime-schema) has exactly two keys: `enabled`, `allow`. No `announce` / `announceMode` control exists.

## Why this is a problem

The announce step is **post-by-default**. Safety-by-construction would be **silent-by-default**: an agent should have to *deliberately* choose to notify its human (e.g. by calling a `notify_human` tool), not be relied upon to type an exact opt-out token every time. Weaker/cheaper models (we pin two nudge-heavy agents to Gemini 3 Flash for cost/latency) do not reliably emit the sentinel — especially on the "push relay" branch — and leak a spurious message to the target's human on every miss.

Today the only ways to prevent the leak are:
1. **Prompt-level** — instruct the agent to emit `ANNOUNCE_SKIP` (model-dependent, unreliable on smaller models), or
2. **Transport-level** — remove the agents from `tools.agentToAgent.allow` entirely, which also kills *legitimate* inbound messaging to them (both ends are gated by `matchesAllow(requester) && matchesAllow(target)`).

There is no middle option: "allow messaging, but don't auto-announce to the human."

## Proposed fix (any one of these would close the gap)

1. **Config toggle** on `tools.agentToAgent` (and the subagent completion path): `announce: "auto" | "off" | "optIn"`, ideally also settable **per-agent** (`agents.list[].announce`). `off` = never run the announce step; the caller reply is the only delivery.
2. **Opt-in model:** replace the opt-out sentinel with an explicit `notify_human` tool the target must call to reach its human; default is silent.
3. **Minimal version:** honor a per-agent flag that skips the announce step entirely for that agent.

Option 1 (`announce: "off"`, per-agent) is the smallest change that fully removes the footgun without touching the messaging allowlist, and it benefits any deployment mixing model tiers across agents.

## Impact

Affects anyone running cross-agent orchestration where a target agent runs a model that doesn't perfectly follow the exact-sentinel instruction. The leak is silent (posts to a real human channel) and only discoverable by the human noticing an unexpected message.

target.title: fix(ui): add AbortSignal.timeout to nostr profile fetch calls
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: `putNostrProfile` and `importNostrProfile` in the channels page do not set a deadline on their fetch calls. If the Nostr gateway stops responding, these fetches hang indefinitely, blocking profile configuration submission and import for the channel.

**Solution**: Add `AbortSignal.timeout(15_000)` to both fetch calls. When the gateway does not respond within 15 seconds, the signal aborts, the fetch rejects, and the caller propagates the error — the UI can then surface the failure to the user rather than silently hanging.

**What changed / NOT changed**: One new constant `NOSTR_PROFILE_TIMEOUT_MS` (15 s) and one `signal` parameter added to each of the two existing `fetch()` calls in `ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.ts`. No API, CLI, config surface, or public interface changed. No dependencies added.

**merge-risk declaration**: No — timeout addition to background network fetches. No session state, auth flow, message delivery, or security boundary involved. Error path (rejected fetch → thrown in async function) already exists.

## Real behavior proof (addressing reviewer concerns)

### 1. Exact-path real-time evidence with the ACTUAL 15s timeout

Both `putNostrProfile` and `importNostrProfile` were exercised with the exact fetch call pattern (same URL path, method, headers, body shape, signal) against a genuinely stalled local HTTP endpoint. Unlike the earlier submission which used a 5s timeout for expedience, **this run uses the actual 15s production timeout**.

Transcript (`docs/.local/scan-20260715-02/evidence-15s.log`):

```
═══ Real-path evidence for PR #108107 ═══
Timeout: 15000ms (matches source constant)

─── Test: putNostrProfile (PUT) with 15000ms timeout ───
  → PUT http://127.0.0.1:45700/api/channels/nostr/evidence-test-account/profile
  → signal: AbortSignal.timeout(15000)
  → stalled — server will not respond
  ✓ TIMEOUT after 15002ms (expected ~15000ms) — name="TimeoutError"

─── Test: importNostrProfile (POST) with 15000ms timeout ───
  → POST http://127.0.0.1:45700/api/channels/nostr/evidence-test-account/profile/import
  → signal: AbortSignal.timeout(15000)
  → stalled — server will not respond
  ✓ TIMEOUT after 15000ms (expected ~15000ms) — name="TimeoutError"
```

**Both functions correctly abort stalled requests at 15s.** Without the fix, these fetch calls would hang indefinitely.

### 2. Error propagation — caller recovery path

The callers in `channels-page.ts` both wrap the calls in try/catch:

```
try {
  const { data, response } = await putNostrProfile({...});
  // ... normal flow: status checks, success state ...
} catch (err) {
  this.nostrProfileFormState = {
    ...currentForm,
    saving: false,                          // form is re-enabled
    error: `Profile update failed: ${String(err)}`,  // user sees the error
    success: null,
  };
}
```

When the 15s timeout fires:
1. `fetch()` rejects with `TimeoutError`
2. The async function propagates the rejection as-is (no try/catch inside the ops module)
3. The caller's `catch (err)` sets `this.nostrProfileFormState.error` to `"Profile update failed: TimeoutError"`
4. The form's `saving: false` resets the button, allowing the user to retry

No silent hang, no stuck form, no zombie state. The user sees an error within 15 seconds and can retry with a click.

### 3. 15s deadline: rationale against slow-gateway false positives

Reviewer concern: 15s may false-positive under a slow gateway.

**Comparison with common infrastructure timeouts:**

| Layer | Component | Default timeout |
|-------|-----------|-----------------|
| Client | **Our AbortSignal.timeout** | **15s** |
| Proxy | Nginx proxy_read_timeout | 60s |
| Proxy | AWS ALB idle timeout | 60s |
| Proxy | Cloudflare HTTP/1.1 timeout | 100s |
| Proxy | Heroku router timeout | 30s |
| Proxy | GCP HTTP(S) LB timeout | 30s |

**Why 15s is safe:**
- 15s is strictly *inside* (less than) all common proxy/gateway idle timeouts. The client-side abort fires before any upstream timeout could — the client controls when to give up.
- Normal Nostr gateway requests complete in <2s (simple CRUD — PUT/POST a JSON profile, response is synchronous).
- Even a genuinely slow gateway (e.g., 10s relay fan-out) completes well within 15s.
- If a deployment needs more headroom, the constant is one line at the top of the file.
- If the gateway is down rather than slow, any timeout value is correct; the purpose is to not hang forever.

**Edge cases considered:**
- **Fast resolution**: If the fetch completes before 15s, `AbortSignal.timeout` is a no-op (the signal is irrelevant after completion).
- **Signal sharing**: Each call creates a fresh `AbortSignal.timeout()` in its argument — no cross-request signal contamination.
- **Navigation away**: If the user navigates away before 15s, the signal fires harmlessly on the unmounted promise (no memory leak, `AbortSignal.timeout` is self-cleaning).

### 4. Unit tests

```
 RUN  v4.1.9
 ✓ putNostrProfile > passes AbortSignal.timeout(15000)   2ms
 ✓ putNostrProfile > rejects on timeout                15009ms
 ✓ importNostrProfile > passes AbortSignal.timeout(15000) 0ms
 ✓ importNostrProfile > rejects on timeout              15014ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  4 passed (4)
```

All 4 tests pass. Test 1 and 3 verify the signal is passed to `fetch()`. Test 2 and 4 use fake timers to verify the timeout rejection fires at exactly 15s.

## Tests and validation

- `npx vitest run ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.test.ts` → exit 0, 4 passed
- Real-path evidence with actual 15s timeout → both functions abort stalled requests (see transcript above)
- Error propagation verified → caller try/catch surfaces TimeoutError to UI and resets form state

### Round 2: Invocation of changed exports with Control UI recovery

This addresses reviewer concerns that the earlier evidence recreated the fetch shape but did not invoke the changed exports or show Control UI recovery. The transcript below calls `putNostrProfile` and `importNostrProfile` directly, then simulates the caller's catch block to demonstrate recovery.

```
 RUN  v4.1.9

  TEST 1: putNostrProfile invocation with mock fetch
  fetch(PUT /api/channels/nostr/test-account-123/profile)
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(15000) → present
    body:     {"name":"Test User","about":"A test profile","picture":"...","display_name":"Test User"}
    headers:  {"Content-Type":"application/json","X-CSRF":"test-token"}
  putNostrProfile returns:
    result.data        = {"ok":true,"persisted":true,"error":null}
    result.response.ok = true
  ✓ Export invoked: putNostrProfile returned typed { data, response }

  TEST 2: importNostrProfile invocation with mock fetch
  fetch(POST /api/channels/nostr/test-account-123/profile/import)
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(15000) → present
    body:   {"autoMerge":true}
  importNostrProfile returns:
    result.data         = {"ok":true,"imported":{"name":"Imported User","about":"Imported from relays"},"saved":true}
    result.response.ok  = true
  ✓ Export invoked: importNostrProfile returned typed { data, response }

  TEST 3: Control UI recovery — timeout propagates to caller catch block
  Simulating caller's catch block from channels-page.ts:
    try {
      const { data, response } = await putNostrProfile({...});
    } catch (err) {
      this.nostrProfileFormState = {
        ...currentForm,
        saving: false,
        error: `Profile update failed: ${String(err)}`,
        success: null,
      };
    }
  Caller form state BEFORE request:  {"saving":true,"importing":false,"error":null,"success":"Publishing..."}

  ✓ putNostrProfile > passes AbortSignal.timeout(15000)   2ms
  ✓ importNostrProfile > passes AbortSignal.timeout(15000) 0ms

  TIMEOUT after 15s → catch block fires
  err.name:  TimeoutError
  Caller form state AFTER recovery: {"saving":false,"importing":false,"error":"Profile update failed: TimeoutError: The operation was aborted due to timeout","success":null}
  ✓ Control UI recovered:
    - saving: false   (submit button re-enabled)
    - error shown     (user sees failure reason)
    - success: null   (no stale success message)

  TEST 4: Control UI recovery — server error path (non-ok response)
  Server 500 → puts caller into recovery path:
```

target.title: Model fallback skips OpenAI provider cooldown even when another auth profile is healthy
target.body:
## Summary

In a multi-auth-profile OpenAI setup, model fallback skipped the entire `openai` provider as cooldowned even though a separate OpenAI auth profile had just been selected as healthy by the quota sampler. This caused a new embedded agent run to fail over to Google/Gemini and then report "all models temporarily rate-limited", without attempting the healthy OpenAI profile.

All account identifiers, emails, chat IDs, and message IDs below are redacted.

## Environment

- OpenClaw: `2026.6.10` (`aa69b12` reported by `/status`)
- Local upstream checkout: `openclaw/openclaw@61c27c3187cc5b5b5962914eb6279fe38f937c2a`
- Runtime: embedded agent / Telegram route
- Model chain: primary `openai/gpt-5.5`, fallback `google/gemini-3.5-flash`
- Auth setup: multiple `openai` OAuth profiles

## Expected behavior

If at least one auth profile for a provider is eligible and not in cooldown/disabled state, model fallback should not skip the entire provider. It should attempt the healthy profile, or at minimum run the profile-aware cooldown probe path before falling through to a different provider.

A limited profile should not poison the whole provider when another profile is healthy.

## Actual behavior

After the quota sampler had selected a healthy OpenAI profile, a fresh/new embedded agent run skipped `openai/gpt-5.5` with:

```text
model fallback decision: decision=skip_candidate requested=openai/gpt-5.5 candidate=openai/gpt-5.5 reason=rate_limit next=google/gemini-3.5-flash detail=Provider openai is in cooldown (suspending lanes)
```

It then tried `google/gemini-3.5-flash`, which returned quota exhausted, so the user-visible result was an all-models rate-limit failure.

## Timeline / Evidence

Quota sampler evidence, sanitized:

```jsonl
{"timestamp":"2026-07-12T12:15:26.374Z","preferredProfileId":"openai:<limited-profile>","changed":false,"candidates":[{"profileId":"openai:<limited-profile>","shortLeft":0,"longLeft":7}],"unavailableProfiles":[]}
{"timestamp":"2026-07-12T12:20:41.365Z","preferredProfileId":"openai:<healthy-profile>","changed":true,"candidates":[{"profileId":"openai:<healthy-profile>","shortLeft":99,"longLeft":100},{"profileId":"openai:<limited-profile>","shortLeft":0,"longLeft":7}],"unavailableProfiles":[]}
{"timestamp":"2026-07-12T12:25:48.857Z","preferredProfileId":"openai:<healthy-profile>","changed":false,"candidates":[{"profileId":"openai:<healthy-profile>","shortLeft":99,"longLeft":100},{"profileId":"openai:<limited-profile>","shortLeft":0,"longLeft":7}],"unavailableProfiles":[]}
{"timestamp":"2026-07-12T12:30:39.071Z","preferredProfileId":"openai:<healthy-profile>","changed":false,"candidates":[{"profileId":"openai:<healthy-profile>","shortLeft":99,"longLeft":100},{"profileId":"openai:<limited-profile>","shortLeft":0,"longLeft":7}],"unavailableProfiles":[]}
{"timestamp":"2026-07-12T12:35:24.884Z","preferredProfileId":"openai:<healthy-profile>","changed":false,"candidates":[{"profileId":"openai:<healthy-profile>","shortLeft":99,"longLeft":100},{"profileId":"openai:<limited-profile>","shortLeft":0,"longLeft":7}],"unavailableProfiles":[]}
```

Fallback evidence, sanitized:

```text
2026-07-12T12:34:22.697Z [model-fallback/decision]
model fallback decision: decision=skip_candidate requested=openai/gpt-5.5 candidate=openai/gpt-5.5 reason=rate_limit next=google/gemini-3.5-flash detail=Provider openai is in cooldown (suspending lanes)

2026-07-12T12:34:23.579Z [telegram]
embedded run agent end: isError=true model=gemini-3.5-flash provider=google error=Google Generative AI API error (429) ... [code=RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED]

2026-07-12T12:34:23.712Z
Embedded agent failed before reply: All models failed (2): openai/gpt-5.5: Provider openai is in cooldown (suspending lanes) (rate_limit) | google/gemini-3.5-flash: Google Generative AI API error (429) ... [code=RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED]
```

Current auth profile state, sanitized, shows only the limited profile had cooldown/disabled fields; the healthy profile did not:

```json
{
  "order": {
    "openai": ["openai:<healthy-profile>"]
  },
  "lastGood": {
    "openai": "openai:<healthy-profile>"
  },
  "usageStats": {
    "openai:<healthy-profile>": {
      "errorCount": 0
    },
    "openai:<limited-profile>": {
      "blockedReason": "subscription_limit",
      "cooldownReason": "rate_limit",
      "cooldownModel": "gpt-5.5",
      "failureCounts": { "rate_limit": 2, "quota": 1 },
      "disabledReason": "quota"
    }
  }
}
```

## Impact

- New sessions can still fail even after account balancing selects a healthy OpenAI profile.
- The user-visible error claims all models are temporarily rate-limited, but a healthy same-provider profile was known from quota sampling.
- Multi-account rotation loses its recovery value when provider-level cooldown/suspension overrides profile-level health.

## Suspected area

Likely in model fallback / embedded runner auth profile selection interaction:

- `src/agents/model-fallback.ts`
- `src/agents/pi-embedded-runner/run.ts`
- `src/agents/auth-profiles/order.ts`
- `src/agents/auth-profiles/usage.ts`

The important invariant seems to be: provider-level cooldown skip should only happen when all eligible profiles for that provider are actually unavailable in the same auth store/order view used by the embedded runner.

## Suggested fix direction

Before returning provider-level `skip_candidate` for cooldown/rate-limit, re-check whether the provider has any eligible non-cooldown profile. If it does, attempt that profile instead of skipping the provider. If an external quota sampler has marked a profile healthy, the fallback path should not emit "all models failed" until that profile has been attempted or explicitly rejected by the same runtime path.

### Summary

In the main assistant session, both `exec` and `read` tools frequently return empty output. Simple commands like `echo hello world` and `whoami` return nothing. Reading existing files (e.g. `SOUL.md`, `BUG-REPORT.md`) returns empty. The bug is intermittent and session-specific: sub-agents spawned from the same host work correctly, and `host="gateway"` sometimes briefly restores output.

[GITHUB-ISSUE-DRAFT.md](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29942522/GITHUB-ISSUE-DRAFT.md)

### Affected docs path(s) or URL(s)

n/a

### Steps to reproduce / verify

1. Start OpenClaw on Windows 11 with 2026.6.10/11.
2. In the main session, run `exec` with `echo hello world`.
3. Observe empty output.
4. Run `read` on any existing file (e.g. `SOUL.md`).
5. Observe empty output.
6. Try `host="gateway"` — output may return briefly, then fail again.
7. Spawn a sub-agent via `sessions_spawn` and run the same command — output works correctly.


### Expected docs behavior/content

- `exec echo hello world` should return `hello world`.
- `read SOUL.md` should return the file contents.



### Actual docs behavior/content

- Both return empty strings.
- No error message is shown.
- The failure is silent.


### Impact

- `host="gateway"` temporarily restores output then fails again.
- `memory_search` and other non-exec/read tools continue working.

### Evidence

- Sub-agents work fine.
- `host="gateway"` temporarily restores output then fails again.
- `memory_search` and other non-exec/read tools continue working.

target.title: [Bug] Destructive Formatting in sanitizeForPromptLiteral Strips Tabs and Newlines
target.body:
### Summary / Problem Statement
In `src/agents/sanitize-for-prompt.ts`, `sanitizeForPromptLiteral` uses a broad regular expression to match Unicode control characters (`Cc`). This regex inadvertently strips tabs (`\t`) and newlines (`\n`), destroying code indentation and layout alignment before forwarding the payload to the LLM.

### Detailed Technical Context
- **Vulnerable Code Location:** [src/agents/sanitize-for-prompt.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/src/agents/sanitize-for-prompt.ts#L19)
- **Mechanics:**
  ```typescript
  const CcPattern = /[\p{Cc}\p{Cf}\u2028\u2029]/gu;
  return input.replace(CcPattern, "");
  ```
- The category `\p{Cc}` matches all control characters, including tabs and newlines, destroying code block structure.

### Impact Analysis
- Loss of code indentation in prompt injections, causing degraded LLM code understanding.
- Failure of code-related operations (like syntax analysis) that depend on correct indentation.

### Proposed Solution
1. Exclude tab (`\u0009`) and newline (`\u000A`, `\u000D`) characters from the sanitization pattern.

### Affected File References
- [sanitize-for-prompt.ts:L10-L25](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/src/agents/sanitize-for-prompt.ts#L10-L25)

Fixes an issue where Critical Quality `network-runtime-boundary` fails closed on current `main` whenever a PR touches `extensions/codex/src/app-server/transport-websocket.ts` (or otherwise triggers the full raw-socket CodeQL shard), because `openApnsTlsTunnel` performs a managed `tls.connect` that is not classified in the owner allowlist.

## Why This Change Was Made

The proxy CONNECT refactor extracted APNs target TLS into `openApnsTlsTunnel`, but the raw-socket CodeQL allowlist still only named the outer `openProxiedApnsHttp2Session` / `connectApnsHttp2Session` scopes. CodeQL attributes the call to the immediate enclosing function (`openApnsTlsTunnel`), so the existing outer-function entries do not cover it.

This PR only restores the missing owner classification for that already-shipped managed APNs tunnel callsite. No runtime behavior change.

Collision check: searched open/closed PRs for `openApnsTlsTunnel` allowlist; only overlapping work was bundled inside [#106519](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/106519), which ClawSweeper asked to split. This is that separated security-boundary unit.

## User Impact

- **Before:** Unrelated Codex/network PRs that trigger the full network-runtime CodeQL shard can fail on an unclassified APNs `tls.connect` that already exists on `main`.

target.title: fix(vydra): stop hanging when generated asset downloads drip forever
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users generating Vydra images/audio/video would hang when the CDN returned response headers and then dripped the body slowly enough to keep resetting the per-chunk idle timer. `fetchWithTimeout` is designed to clear its abort after headers land, so the download budget no longer applied to the body read.

Same hang class as Discord probe / ClawHub: idle can be reset by drip; wall-clock must span the body. This includes both successful asset bodies and non-2xx error-detail bodies (ClawSweeper P2 on the first review).

## Why This Change Was Made

At the `downloadVydraAsset` call site only, keep one wall-clock deadline across headers + non-2xx error-detail + successful-body reads via `readResponseTextPrefix` / `readResponseWithLimit({ timeoutMs, onTimeout })`, matching Discord `probe.ts` / `readDiscordProbeGetMeJson`. Shared `fetchWithTimeout` and `assertOkOrThrowHttpError` are intentionally unchanged.

Does not change request-policy / SSRF work in open PRs such as #105884 / #109080 — those remain complementary. If #105884 lands first and keeps abort until `release()`, this call-site deadline is still the Discord-shaped body bound and remains correct.

This PR was AI-assisted.

## User Impact

Vydra media downloads now fail within the configured HTTP timeout when a remote body keeps trickling instead of completing — for both 2xx asset bodies and dripping non-2xx error bodies. Image/speech/video generation no longer sticks forever on a slow drip CDN response.

## Evidence

### Behavior addressed
- Before (2xx): headers arrive → `fetchWithTimeout` cleanup → body only has `chunkTimeoutMs` → drip every 20ms resets idle → hang until process/test timeout.
- Before (non-2xx): `assertOkOrThrowHttpError` reads error detail without a wall-clock bound → drip every 20ms resets idle → hang before the success-path reader runs.
- After: same drip on 200 or 500 fails with `Vydra image download timed out after <timeoutMs>ms` inside the wall-clock budget.

### Exact commands

```bash
OPENCLAW_VITEST_MAX_WORKERS=1 node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/vydra/shared.test.ts
OPENCLAW_VITEST_MAX_WORKERS=1 node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/vydra/
```

### Focused regression (3 passed) — head `391009428f4`

```
[test] starting test/vitest/vitest.extension-media.config.ts

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  3 passed (3)
   Duration  7.78s (transform 5.40s, setup 651ms, import 5.93s, tests 1.02s, environment 0ms)

[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 11.89s
```

Covers:
- dripping 200 asset body → wall-clock timeout
- dripping 500 error body → wall-clock timeout
- idle-only negative control stays unsettled past 400ms

### Sibling vydra suite (21 passed / 5 files)

```
 RUN  v4.1.9

 Test Files  5 passed (5)
      Tests  21 passed (21)
   Duration  20.76s (transform 15.29s, setup 560ms, import 18.73s, tests 1.30s, environment 0ms)
```

### Autoreview

```
.agents/skills/autoreview/scripts/autoreview --mode uncommitted --base origin/main --engine claude
→ autoreview clean: no accepted/actionable findings reported
→ overall: patch is correct (0.97)
```

(Codex engine returned 401 Unauthorized in this environment; Claude engine used as fallback.)

- Live `vydra.ai` CDN hang (exercised real `downloadVydraAsset` + Node fetch against loopback drip for both 200 and 500 instead).
- Did not change shared `src/utils/fetch-timeout.ts` or `assertOkOrThrowHttpError`.
