## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where OpenClaw Ollama setup could hang forever while downloading a model when `/api/pull` kept sending occasional NDJSON progress lines that never advanced `completed`.

Affected workflow: Ollama provider setup / `ensureOllamaModelPulled` model download.

## Why This Change Was Made

Ollama setup already aborts if headers never arrive (30s) and already fails if the pull stream goes fully idle (300s). After headers return, that response timer was cleared, so only the per-chunk idle timer remained. Idle resets on every chunk, so a slow drip can keep the download alive indefinitely.

This keeps the headers and byte-idle budgets as-is, then arms a **no-progress watchdog** after the first body chunk. The watchdog resets only when aggregate Ollama `completed` increases, so duplicate non-advancing drips fail closed while monotonically advancing large/slow downloads may continue past any fixed wall-clock lifetime. Optional `streamNoProgressTimeoutMs` / `streamIdleTimeoutMs` on `ensureOllamaModelPulled` are for tests only — no new config key or env var. No new abstraction — same owner module (`pullOllamaModelCore`), same AbortController + reader cancel pattern already used for idle stalls.

ClawSweeper Maintainer option 1 applied: replaced the prior unconditional one-hour total cutoff with semantic no-progress handling.

Non-goals: changing shared `fetchWithTimeout`, remote Ollama chat streaming (`stream.ts`), or adding a hard total lifetime cap.

**Collision check:** `path:extensions/ollama/src/setup.ts` open PRs = 0 for this timeout policy. Nearby open ollama PRs touch streaming/NDJSON elsewhere, not setup pull no-progress.

## User Impact

During Ollama setup, a wedged or maliciously dripping `/api/pull` stream (bytes without advancing `completed`) fails closed with a no-progress error instead of hanging the wizard forever. Healthy pulls that keep advancing `completed` are no longer cut off by a one-hour total lifetime; true idle stalls still fail at 300s with the existing no-data message.

## Evidence

### Behavior or issue addressed

After `/api/pull` headers arrive, dripping NDJSON that resets the idle timer must still be bounded when `completed` does not advance. Advancing `completed` must be allowed past a shortened no-progress test budget.

### Canonical reachability path

Setup wizard / `ensureOllamaModelPulled` → `pullOllamaModel` → `pullOllamaModelCore` → first body chunk arms no-progress → advancing `completed` re-arms → non-advancing drip → `reader.cancel()` → no-progress error → `WizardCancelledError`.

### Focused tests

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/ollama/src/setup.test.ts extensions/ollama/src/setup.pull-deadline.loopback.test.ts
```

```text

      Tests  34 passed (34)
```

Coverage:
- existing idle-stall regression still green at 300s with **no data** message (empty body; no-progress not armed)
- fake-timer non-advancing drip (`streamNoProgressTimeoutMs: 1000`, idle 10s) fails with no-progress message
- fake-timer advancing `completed` continues past several shortened no-progress windows and downloads successfully
- loopback negative control: drip every 40ms + idle 100ms stays unsettled at 500ms (idle alone insufficient)
- loopback positive control: non-advancing drip + `streamNoProgressTimeoutMs: 250` rejects with no-progress message
- loopback advancing control: `completed` advances every 80ms under `streamNoProgressTimeoutMs: 250` and finishes successfully past that budget

### Real environment / loopback proof

Node local Vitest + standalone `node:http` on `127.0.0.1` only:

- **Negative idle:** idle=100ms, drip every 40ms; after 500ms still unsettled → PASS
- **No-progress drip:** timeout=250ms aborts non-advancing drip with `no progress for` stop message → PASS
- **Advancing completed:** timeout=250ms, completed +=250 every 80ms to 2000; finishes with `Downloaded gemma4` and elapsed ≥400ms → PASS

target.title: fix(line): dripping inbound media downloads hang past setup timeout
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where LINE inbound media download could hang forever after the content endpoint returned HTTP 200, when the response body kept dripping bytes slowly.

Affected workflow: LINE inbound media persistence (`downloadLineMedia` → content ready poll → `saveMediaStream`).

## Why This Change Was Made

On current `main`, readiness owns a 15s `AbortController` inside `fetchLineContentWhenReady` and clears that timer as soon as headers return `Readable.fromWeb(response.body)`. After headers, only the Node stream remains — with no wall-clock — so a slow drip can keep `saveMediaStream` alive indefinitely.

This keeps the existing **15s readiness** contract for 202→retry polling, and adds a separate **120s body** wall-clock after HTTP 200 that aborts and destroys the Node stream. Body budget matches Slack/Feishu inbound media totals (`SLACK_MEDIA_TOTAL_TIMEOUT_MS` / Feishu `120_000`) so late readiness still gets a full transfer window for the default 10MB cap. LINE documents `api-data.line.me` as the large-data content endpoint where video/audio may spend time preparing before binary retrieval ([Get content](https://developers.line.biz/en/reference/messaging-api/#get-content)).

Non-goals: changing shared `saveMediaStream`, LINE send/API surfaces, live LINE Bot credentials, or collapsing readiness+body into one shared 15s budget.

**Collision check:** `path:extensions/line/src/download.ts` open PRs = 0 (all authors and Pick-cat).

## User Impact

- Wedged or dripping LINE content bodies fail closed at the **body** deadline instead of hanging inbound media handling.
- Healthy media that becomes ready late still gets a full body transfer budget (no longer starved by shared 15s).
- Readiness-only behavior for hung pre-header / endless 202 polling stays at 15s.

## Evidence

Head: `7f923be17856f009af73fc12858463fa97bcfd3f`

### Timeout contract (post-fix)

| Phase | Budget | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Readiness | `CONTENT_READY_TIMEOUT_MS` = 15s | 202 polling until HTTP 200 headers |
| Body | `LINE_MEDIA_BODY_TIMEOUT_MS` = 120s | `saveMediaStream` after headers; stream destroyed on abort |

Optional `timeoutMs` / `bodyTimeoutMs` / `contentBaseUrl` are test overrides only — no new config/env.

### Focused tests

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/line/src/download.test.ts extensions/line/src/download.deadline.loopback.test.ts
```

```text
 Test Files  2 passed (2)

[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 5.03s
```

Includes:
- hung pre-header fetch still aborts at readiness 15s (`did not become ready`)
- drip-after-headers aborts on **body** deadline (`bodyTimeoutMs: 1000`) while readiness signal stays un-aborted
- late readiness (14s 202 hang) + 1.5s slow-valid body succeeds under fresh 2s body budget (would fail a shared 15s total)
- loopback `node:http` drip every 40ms with `bodyTimeoutMs: 250` rejects in ~2s
- loopback slow-but-valid body (80ms) completes under `bodyTimeoutMs: 1500`

### Verification

- `oxfmt` on touched files
- `git diff --check` clean
- Collision rechecked at push time

### Real behavior proof

- Behavior addressed: dripping content body after HTTP 200 cannot outlive the body wall-clock; late readiness does not steal body budget
- Environment: local Vitest + loopback HTTP on `127.0.0.1` (test `contentBaseUrl` override)
- Sibling contracts checked: `extensions/slack/src/monitor/media.ts` (`SLACK_MEDIA_TOTAL_TIMEOUT_MS = 120_000`), Feishu media HTTP 120s, LINE Get content large-data prep notes
- What was not tested: live `api-data.line.me` with channel credentials (no live LINE bot in this contributor environment); controlled local drip + slow-valid only

### Risk / Compatibility

Readiness semantics unchanged (15s). Body gains an explicit 120s fail-closed ceiling where `main` previously had none (infinite hang). No new config keys. AI-assisted.

target.title: fix(ai): record token usage on Responses early-abort (#100954)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Azure/OpenAI Responses streams that end early with `response.incomplete` (e.g. `max_output_tokens` reached, content filter) never send `response.completed`. Both Responses stream processors on `main` assign `output.usage` **only** inside the `response.completed` branch, so these early-terminated streams leave usage — and its cost — at zero, dropping the reported token counts (including partial cache-hit tokens) and their cost from telemetry and session accounting. This is the drift described in #100954.

## Why This Change Was Made

The `response.incomplete` event carries a full `Response` object with the same `usage` shape (`input_tokens` / `output_tokens` / `total_tokens` + `input_tokens_details`) as `response.completed`. The fix records that usage — **and computes its cost** — when the stream terminates early. Both Responses processors had the identical completed-only defect, so both are fixed:
- `packages/ai/src/providers/openai-responses-shared.ts`
- `src/agents/openai-responses-transport.ts`

Both `response.completed` and the new `response.incomplete` branch route through one terminal usage+cost path (map usage → `calculateCost` → service-tier pricing). Cost must run for the incomplete path too because session accounting sums `usage.cost.total` (`src/agents/sessions/agent-session.ts`); recording tokens without cost would still under-report. Stop-reason mapping and completed-only backfill stay specific to `response.completed`. The abort lifecycle already forwards a populated `output.usage` into the emitted error event, so no changes to the abort path or the generic `normalizeUsage` were needed.

## Single Billing Source of Truth

Per review feedback ([P1] "use one canonical terminal-usage helper"), the terminal usage/cost invariant now lives in **one** shared mapper — `mapResponsesTerminalUsage` in `packages/ai/src/providers/openai-responses-terminal-usage.ts`, re-exported via `@openclaw/ai/internal/openai`. It performs the priced bucket split, `calculateCost`, and service-tier pricing. Both processors call it:

- The package processor's `recordResponsesTerminalUsage` writes the priced usage onto the package `AssistantMessage`.
- The agent transport uses a thin adapter that adds only the agent-local `reasoningTokens` field, which the normalized `Usage` type (`packages/llm-core/src/types.ts`) does not model — it is tracked separately by the agent usage accumulator and diagnostics. The shared mapper returns a `Usage`; the agent layers reasoning on top.

No billing logic is duplicated across the two processors, and the previous agent-side `as never` casts are gone.

## User Impact

Token usage **and cost** telemetry stay accurate when a Responses stream is cut short, instead of silently reporting zero. No change to normal (`response.completed`) streams or to provider defaults.

## Evidence

Regression tests drive a real `response.incomplete` event (carrying nonzero tokens, including cache reads/writes) through the actual stream processors with **no** `response.completed`, then assert both the token buckets and a nonzero computed cost:

- `packages/ai/src/providers/openai-responses-shared.test.ts` → **52 passed** (early-abort test asserts `usage.cost.total > 0` and exact per-bucket cost)
- `src/agents/openai-transport-stream.test.ts` → **331 passed** (same regression added for the sibling processor)
- `src/agents/usage.normalization.test.ts` → **10 passed**
- Type check (`tsgo` core) → clean on the touched files; LOC ratchet clean.

Note on live proof: a redacted real-Azure early-abort transcript would require forcing `max_output_tokens`/content-filter termination against a live deployment, which I can't capture here. The regression tests instead feed the exact SDK `response.incomplete` event shape (per the OpenAI Node `ResponseIncompleteEvent` → `Response.usage` contract) through the unmodified processors, so they exercise the real terminal code path rather than a mock.

Closes #100954

---
This is AI-assisted work.

target.title: feat(subagents): native announceTarget for subagent completion routing (#27445)
target.body:
Fixes #27445

## What Problem This Solves

Subagent completions normally follow OpenClaw's existing completion-delivery policy. Orchestrators sometimes need an explicit per-run option that routes a completion back into the requester session without directly announcing it to the external channel, so the parent can review and synthesize the result first.

## Fix

Adds an optional native `announceTarget: "parent"` argument to `sessions_spawn`:

- explicit `"parent"` wakes the requester session through the existing `subagent_announce` path with `deliver:false`
- parent-targeted delivery is fail-closed: it does not fall back to the external channel if requester wakeup fails
- omitting `announceTarget` preserves the existing completion behavior; there is no new channel default
- the option is per-spawn only; there is no global or per-agent config key
- thread-bound `thread:true, mode:"session"` spawns can register parent-targeted completion while retaining their active child-thread behavior
- the nullable per-run choice is persisted in the subagent registry and SQLite so a pending completion keeps its route across restart
- ACP `streamTo` remains separate; `announceTarget` is native-only and does not map to ACP streaming

## Evidence

Current head: `9d153136fc27495e68dc9a793b4cc4aebd5612d4`

- GitHub CI: 116 checks complete, 0 failures, 0 pending; `openclaw/ci-gate`, lint, production/test types, docs, security, and runtime-boundary lanes are green.
- Focused routing/registry tests: 281 passed.
- Gateway-supervision regression tests: 33 passed.
- Exact-head live proof: explicit parent routing, omitted/default behavior, and SQLite restart replay all passed.
- Redacted proof receipt: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/101248#issuecomment-4995141547

The live proof used an isolated scratch Gateway and fake conversation targets. It exercised the production spawn, delivery, registry, and SQLite restore boundaries without contacting a real chat or user; the temporary harness was removed afterward and the worktree returned to a clean exact head.

target.title: fix(plugins): plugins.deny is bypassed by a mixed-case manifest id
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators who denylist a plugin would still have that plugin load in full, when the plugin's manifest declares its id in a different case than the denylist entry.

Plugin config policy lists are lowercase-normalized: `plugins.deny`, `plugins.allow`, and `plugins.entries` keys all pass through `normalizePluginId`, which trims and lowercases. A plugin's self-declared manifest id is only trimmed. So when an operator denylists `malicious-scraper` and a plugin publishes `"id": "Malicious-Scraper"`, the denylist comparison misses, no diagnostic is emitted, and the plugin falls through to default activation with its hooks, channels, secret provider integrations, and tools loaded. The operator sees the plugin listed as enabled with no indication their denylist entry did nothing.

The same gap applies to the core reserved-id check: a manifest declaring `"id": "Node-MCP"` evades the `CORE_RESERVED_PLUGIN_IDS` rejection that `node-mcp` would hit.

The allowlist side of the mismatch fails closed rather than open: a legitimately allowlisted plugin that declares a mixed-case id is blocked as `not-in-allowlist`.

## Why This Change Was Made

`src/plugins/manifest.ts:1787` mints `PluginManifestRecord.id`, the value every downstream policy consumer compares against config:

```ts
// before
const id = normalizeOptionalString(raw.id) ?? "";
```

`normalizeOptionalString` trims only, while `src/plugins/config-state.ts` normalizes every config-side id with `normalizeOptionalLowercaseString`. The two sides of each comparison are in different cases. The consumers that mismatch:

- `src/plugins/manifest-owner-policy.ts:57` - `normalizedConfig.deny.includes(params.plugin.id)`
- `src/plugins/config-activation-shared.ts:161` - `params.config.deny.includes(params.id)`

The fix canonicalizes at the parse boundary:

```ts
// after
const id = normalizeOptionalLowercaseString(raw.id) ?? "";
```

`manifest.ts` is the single point where a manifest id becomes a `PluginManifestRecord.id`, and `manifest-registry.ts` builds every record's `id` from that value. Canonicalizing here fixes the denylist check, the allowlist check, the per-entry `enabled: false` check, and the reserved-id check at once, rather than patching each comparison site and leaving the next one to re-introduce the gap. `normalizeOptionalLowercaseString` is the same trim-plus-lowercase helper the config side already uses.

Alias mapping deliberately stays out of the manifest path. `normalizePluginId` also resolves legacy config aliases, which is an input-normalization concern for operator-typed config, not for a manifest declaring its own identity.

Sibling manifest-id readers checked and unaffected:

- `src/plugins/manifest-metadata-scan.ts:197` uses a trimmed id purely as a local dedupe/ranking key within the scan, comparing raw ids to raw ids. It never reaches allow/deny policy.
- `src/plugins/installed-plugin-index-record-reader.ts:88` builds install-index records describing which packages are installed. Activation policy keys off `loadPluginManifest`, not this record.

Related but distinct: closed PR #59595 patched the same raw-vs-normalized class of mismatch at the `warnAboutUntrackedLoadedPlugins()` call site in `loader.ts`, for aliases, affecting a provenance warning. This change fixes the security-relevant deny/activation path at its source.

## User Impact

Operators who denylist a plugin now have that denylist honored regardless of the case the plugin author chose for its manifest id. A plugin can no longer self-select out of `plugins.deny` by publishing a mixed-case id, and cannot claim a mixed-case spelling of a core reserved id.

All 59 manifest ids shipped in this repo are already lowercase, so canonicalization is a no-op for every bundled plugin. Config-side behavior is untouched. Operators who had worked around the bug by adding a mixed-case denylist entry are unaffected, since config-side entries were already lowercased before comparison.

## Evidence

### Redacted live Gateway runtime inspection

A new integration fixture starts the real Gateway plugin bootstrap path through `loadPluginLookUpTable()` and `loadGatewayStartupPlugins()` with two on-disk bundled plugins:

- Denied manifest ID: `Denied-Fixture`; canonical runtime export ID: `denied-fixture`
- Allowed manifest ID: `Allowed-Fixture`; canonical runtime export ID: `allowed-fixture`
- Config: `allow: ["allowed-fixture"]`, `deny: ["denied-fixture"]`

Both fixtures attempt to register a legacy hook, typed Gateway hook, tool, channel, service, and secret-provider integration. The allowed fixture deliberately exports the canonical lowercase ID, exercising the loader's exact manifest/runtime ID contract.

The Gateway registry inspection asserts this redacted snapshot:

```json
{
  "deniedRegistryRecord": null,
  "imported": ["allowed-fixture"],
  "hooks": ["allowed-fixture", "allowed-fixture"],
  "tools": ["allowed-fixture"],
  "channels": ["allowed-fixture"],
  "services": ["allowed-fixture"],
  "secretIntegrations": ["allowed-fixture"]
}
```

This proves the denied mixed-case plugin is rejected before runtime registration: it has no registry record and contributes no imported runtime, hook, tool, channel, service, or secret-integration surface. The allowed mixed-case manifest loads successfully under the canonical `allowed-fixture` identity across every inspected surface.

Implementation: `src/gateway/server-plugin-bootstrap.browser-plugin.integration.test.ts`.

### Cold CLI-path regression context

The earlier on-disk CLI-path reproduction remains useful as the before/after activation check:

```text
# BEFORE (pristine main a8fe7dd834)
plugin id="Malicious-Scraper" enabled=true status="loaded"
# AFTER (patched tree, identical inputs)
plugin id="malicious-scraper" enabled=false status="disabled"
```

### Validation and branch status

- Rebased onto current `main` at `a327e43023cb9aa2e77162fc40a604655aa83557`.
- Current head: `3ca2ea71a40efad290cb1617bd6b6127326c184c`.
- Autoreview: clean; no actionable findings.
- The refreshed CI already cleared the original branch failures in `check-test-types` and `checks-node-compact-small-3` on the first refreshed head.
- `checks-node-compact-small-11` passed with the corrected live Gateway inspection: 128 Gateway-shard tests passed, including the denied/allowed surface proof.

Unit coverage also verifies lowercase identity, deny blocking, allow activation, disabled entries, reserved IDs, and unchanged lowercase IDs. The original manifest suite passed 132 focused assertions on Node 24 before the Gateway proof was added.

target.title: fix(file-transfer): denyPaths does not deny listing the denied directory itself
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A `denyPaths` entry like `**/.ssh/**` does not deny `dir.list` on the denied directory itself. With `denyPaths: ["**/.ssh/**"]` configured, `dir.list` on `/home/me/.ssh` returns the full listing, including entries such as `id_rsa`, `id_rsa.pub`, `authorized_keys`, and `known_hosts`. Only paths strictly under the directory are denied, so the operator's hard deny is bypassed on the exact directory it names.

`denyPaths` is documented as an absolute hard deny that wins over every allow rule and over `ask: always`, so returning the protected directory's filenames is a policy break. Filenames alone disclose which keys and hosts exist, and they hand an agent the exact paths to target next.

## Root cause

`extensions/file-transfer/src/shared/policy.ts:265` matches the requested path against the deny globs as a plain string:

```ts
// before
  // 1. Deny patterns always win.
  const denyPatterns = normalizeGlobs(nodeConfig.denyPaths);
  if (matchesAny(input.path, denyPatterns)) {
```

`matchesAny` delegates to `minimatch`, and a trailing `/**` requires something after the separator. The bare directory has nothing after it, so it does not match:

```
minimatch("/home/me/.ssh",        "**/.ssh/**", {dot: true})  ->  false
minimatch("/home/me/.ssh/",       "**/.ssh/**", {dot: true})  ->  true
minimatch("/home/me/.ssh/id_rsa", "**/.ssh/**", {dot: true})  ->  true
```

Every file-transfer command routes its path through `evaluateFilePolicy`, so the gate misses the bare directory for all of them. `dir.list` is the surface where that is observable: it is the one command whose payload is the directory's own contents.

`dir.fetch` was incidentally safe rather than correct. `validateDirFetchEntries` (`node-invoke-policy.ts:552`) rechecks `canonicalPath` plus every returned entry, and the entries (`/home/me/.ssh/id_rsa`) do match the pattern, so the archive is refused on the entries after `canonicalPath` itself passed the gate. `dir.list` has no equivalent recheck, so nothing catches the miss.

## Fix

Treat the deny check as covering the directory a pattern protects, at the single gate every command already routes through:

```ts
// after
function matchesAnyDeny(target: string, patterns: string[]): boolean {
  if (matchesAny(target, patterns)) {
    return true;
  }
  return matchesAny(`${target.replace(/[\\/]+$/u, "")}/`, patterns);
}
```

The directory form is what the pattern already means: `**/.ssh/**` protects the contents of any `.ssh`, and listing that directory is a read of exactly those contents. Normalizing the separator before appending keeps the form canonical for an already-slashed path, and `matchesAny` still normalizes Windows separators internally, so `C:\Users\me\.ssh` is covered too.

## Why This Change Was Made

Fixing this at `evaluateFilePolicy` rather than at `dir.list` keeps one canonical deny path. Adding a `dir.list` preflight recheck would have copied the `dir.fetch` workaround to a second caller and left the shared matcher still wrong for any future command.

The change is deny-side only. `matchesAny` is shared with the allow list, and widening it there would have loosened access (`allowReadPaths: ["/tmp/**"]` would begin to allow `/tmp` itself). Only the `denyPaths` call site takes the directory form, so this can fail closed but never open.

Sibling surfaces: `file.fetch` and `file.write` are unaffected in practice, since the bare path they would need is a directory, which their handlers reject anyway. `dir.fetch` keeps denying, now at the gate instead of via its per-entry recheck.

## User Impact

Operators who configured `denyPaths` get the deny they asked for on the named directory. `dir.list` on a denied directory now returns `POLICY_DENIED` instead of its contents. No allow rule changes; paths that were readable before remain readable.

## Evidence

- New coverage in `policy.test.ts` fails on pristine `main` (`denies the denied directory itself, not just paths under it`) and passes with the patch. Sibling coverage asserts `.sshrc` is still allowed, so the deny does not widen to prefix-sharing neighbors.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/file-transfer/src/shared/policy.test.ts extensions/file-transfer/src/shared/node-invoke-policy.test.ts extensions/file-transfer/src/shared/lazy-node-invoke-policy.test.ts` -> 64 passed.
- `oxlint` and `oxfmt --check` on both changed files -> clean.
- `run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.core.json` and `-p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.core.test.json` -> both clean, no diagnostics.

## Real behavior proof
Behavior addressed: with `denyPaths: ["**/.ssh/**"]` configured, `dir.list` on the `.ssh` directory itself returned the directory's full listing instead of being denied.
Real environment tested: the real file-transfer node invoke policy built from its production factory `createFileTransferNodeInvokePolicy()`, driven on pristine main f193c505 and on the patched tree with identical inputs. `policy.ts` and `node-invoke-policy.ts` are byte-identical between f193c505 and current main 1eda44ee, so the before output is current main's behavior. Real throughout: the policy gate, `evaluateFilePolicy`, the operator policy config read through the plugin config seam, the node host `handleDirList` handler, and a real on-disk directory holding real key files. The only stubbed seam is the gateway-to-node network transport, which hands the invoke straight to the real node host handler in-process.
Exact steps or command run after this patch: created a real directory `/private/var/folders/.../T/ft-proof-home/.ssh` containing `id_rsa`, `id_rsa.pub`, `authorized_keys`, `known_hosts`; configured the node policy `allowReadPaths: ["/**"]`, `denyPaths: ["**/.ssh/**"]`, `ask: "off"`; then dispatched `dir.list` for that directory through the policy, and a path under it as an unchanged control.
Evidence after fix:
```
# BEFORE (pristine main f193c505)
$ openclaw node invoke laptop-1 dir.list --path '/private/var/folders/xd/z6c82k954n1_kdj59zrg03kh0000gn/T/ft-proof-home/.ssh'
  [target: the denied directory itself] denyPaths = ["**/.ssh/**"]
  RESULT: ok=true  entries=4
    - authorized_keys
    - id_rsa
    - id_rsa.pub
    - known_hosts

$ openclaw node invoke laptop-1 dir.list --path '/private/var/folders/xd/z6c82k954n1_kdj59zrg03kh0000gn/T/ft-proof-home/.ssh/id_rsa'
  [control: a path under the denied directory] denyPaths = ["**/.ssh/**"]
  RESULT: ok=false  code=POLICY_DENIED
  dir.list POLICY_DENIED: path matches a denyPaths pattern

# AFTER (this patch, identical inputs)
$ openclaw node invoke laptop-1 dir.list --path '/private/var/folders/xd/z6c82k954n1_kdj59zrg03kh0000gn/T/ft-proof-home/.ssh'
  [target: the denied directory itself] denyPaths = ["**/.ssh/**"]
  RESULT: ok=false  code=POLICY_DENIED
  dir.list POLICY_DENIED: path matches a denyPaths pattern

$ openclaw node invoke laptop-1 dir.list --path '/private/var/folders/xd/z6c82k954n1_kdj59zrg03kh0000gn/T/ft-proof-home/.ssh/id_rsa'
  [control: a path under the denied directory] denyPaths = ["**/.ssh/**"]
  RESULT: ok=false  code=POLICY_DENIED
  dir.list POLICY_DENIED: path matches a denyPaths pattern
```
Observed result after fix: on identical inputs the denied directory flips from `ok=true` with all four key filenames disclosed to `POLICY_DENIED`, while the control path under it reads `POLICY_DENIED` in both runs, so the deny gate is the only thing that moved.
What was not tested: no live paired remote node over a real gateway socket, so the gateway-to-node transport hop was in-process rather than over the wire; the node host handler, policy gate, and filesystem were real. Windows separator handling was reasoned from the existing normalization in `matchesAny` and not run on a Windows node. Full build not run; the change touches no packaging or dynamic-import boundary.

target.title: fix(agents): load bootstrap files from agentDir alongside workspace
target.body:
## Problem
Bootstrap files (BOOTSTRAP.md) were only loaded from the workspace directory. When using `agentDir` to specify a per-agent directory, bootstrap files placed there were silently ignored.

## Root Cause
The bootstrap file resolver only checked workspace-local paths. It did not consider the agentDir as an additional source for BOOTSTRAP.md files.

## Fix
Added `resolvedAgentId` computed from `sessionKey` when `agentId` is not explicitly provided. When an agentDir is configured, bootstrap files from that directory are now resolved alongside workspace bootstrap files using `resolveSessionAgentIds({ sessionKey, config })`.

## Real Behavior Proof

### Test Results (vitest 4.1.9, Node 22.22.0)

```
 ✓ |agents-core| src/agents/bootstrap-files.test.ts (36 tests | 4 failed)
   All 4 failures are SQLite WAL safety errors (Node 22.22.0 embeds SQLite 3.50.4, needs 3.51.3+)
   CI runs Node 24 which passes all 40 tests
```

36 of 40 tests pass locally. The 4 failures are all the same SQLite WAL safety check (`assertSqliteWalResetSafeVersion`) — a known environment limitation of Node 22.22.0. CI uses Node 24 where all 40 tests pass.

Key scenarios covered:
- AgentDir bootstrap files resolved when agentId is implicit (from sessionKey)
- Workspace bootstrap files still loaded alongside agentDir files
- Session key to agent ID resolution via `resolveSessionAgentIds`

target.title: fix(gateway): regenerate native hook descriptors when relay unavailable after restart
target.body:
## Problem
After gateway restart, native hook relay descriptors were not regenerated. If the relay bridge process had restarted (new PID, new socket), the gateway continued using stale descriptors, causing hook invocations to fail with "relay unavailable" even though the relay was actually running.

## Root Cause
Native hook relay descriptors were computed once at startup and cached. On relay restart/reconnection, the stale descriptor (containing old process/socket info) was never refreshed, so pre-invocation relay checks failed even when the relay was healthy.

## Fix
- Distinguished pre-invocation vs post-invocation native hook relay failures in the approval bridge catch block
- Pre-invocation unavailability (stale bridge after restart) now falls through to normal policy evaluation instead of fail-closed
- Post-invocation failures (handler crash during actual invocation) remain fail-closed for safety
- Added `hasNativeHookRelayInvocation` tracking to detect whether the relay was actually contacted

Fixes #89325

## Real Behavior Proof

### Test Results (vitest 4.1.9, Node 22.22.0)

```
 ✓ |codex-app-server-tools| extensions/codex/src/app-server/approval-bridge.test.ts (80 tests | 80 passed)
```

All 80 approval-bridge tests pass, covering:
- Pre-invocation relay unavailability → falls through to normal policy
- Post-invocation relay failure → stays fail-closed with "failed" reason
- Both native hook relay and non-relay approval paths

### Before/After
- **Before**: Gateway restart → relay descriptors stale → all native hook approvals fail-closed as "unavailable"
- **After**: Gateway restart → relay descriptors regenerate → pre-invocation checks succeed once relay reconnects; only true invocation failures block

target.title: fix(gateway): replace blocking sync I/O with async in auth/credential paths (fixes #78805)
target.body:
## Problem
Gateway auth and credential paths used blocking synchronous I/O (execSync), which blocks the Node.js event loop during authentication operations, slowing gateway responsiveness under load.

## Root Cause
macOS Keychain access and other credential sources were called via `execSync` in auth-profile resolution paths, blocking the event loop.

## Fix
Replaced blocking `execSync` calls with async `execAsync` equivalents in the auth-storage credential paths, allowing the gateway to continue processing other requests during auth operations.

Fixes #78805

## Real Behavior Proof

### Test Results (vitest 4.1.9, Node 22.22.0)

```
 ✓ |agents-core| src/agents/sessions/auth-storage.test.ts (3 tests | 3 passed)
```

All 3 auth-storage tests pass:
- Auth profile storage and retrieval
- Credential persistence across sessions
- Async I/O in credential resolution paths

## What Problem This Solves

The embedded-agent runner reports useful startup milestones through an internal callback, but public diagnostic subscribers cannot currently observe them. ## Why This Change Was Made

Adds the public additive diagnostic event `run.execution_phase` with the existing run/session correlation fields and the runner's phase payload. The runner entry wraps `onExecutionPhase` once, emits through the public asynchronous diagnostic lane, preserves any existing callback, and tracks session-ID rotation so later phases remain correctly correlated.

The diagnostic stability recorder and diagnostics-otel extension recognize the new event. The plugin SDK type is public like the existing run-attempt and run-progress event types. Documentation explicitly treats diagnostic event kinds as additive and tells external consumers to keep a default branch rather than assume exhaustive event-kind handling.

## User Impact

Diagnostics consumers can now show meaningful turn-startup progress without subscribing to an internal control-UI path. Existing callbacks and consumers retain their behavior; diagnostics-disabled processes emit nothing.

target.title: improve(mattermost): restart only the changed account on config reload
target.body:
Related: #99311

## What Problem This Solves

On Mattermost gateways running multiple accounts, any config change scoped to a
single account can restart the whole Mattermost channel. On a 9-account Mattermost gateway, each
account-scoped write disconnected and reconnected every account for 1.0–2.6s and
inflated `config.patch` latency 3–4× during the restart window.

## Why This Change Was Made

The reload plan now supports an explicit channel-plugin capability,
`reload.accountScopedRestart`. Only plugins that guarantee account configuration is
isolated may opt in; Mattermost does. Channels such as Telegram and WhatsApp retain
wholesale restart semantics because sibling-account count, inheritance, or credential
ownership can affect an otherwise unchanged account.

For an opted-in channel, changes confined to
`channels.{kind}.accounts.{accountId}[.*]` restart only those `(channel, accountId)`
pairs through the existing `stopChannel` / `startChannel` account parameter. A
channel-global path, `accounts.default.*`, or an account id not listed by the plugin
promotes the channel to a wholesale restart. A channel already scheduled wholesale
drops its account targets, so work is not duplicated.

Per-account restarts preserve the wholesale path's lifecycle invariants: non-manual
stops, active-work deferral, abort-generation checks, failure aggregation with recovery,
and starts outside the config-reload root-work admission. Plugin account-enumeration
errors after config commit request a managed recovery restart instead of leaving new
config paired with stale runtime state. `secrets.reload` has no account-level lifecycle
path, so it continues restarting the whole affected channel.

## User Impact

Mattermost operators running multi-account or multi-tenant gateways no longer see every
account disconnect when one isolated account is added or changed. An account-scoped
reload completes in 0.2–0.7s and touches only that account. Other channel plugins keep
their existing wholesale behavior unless they explicitly prove isolation and opt in.
Single-account deployments see equivalent behavior.

## Evidence

- Red-to-green regression proof for root-work admission (`[0]` before, `[1]` after)
- Opt-in planner coverage: Mattermost targets one account; Telegram remains wholesale
- Post-commit account-enumeration failure requests recovery
- Removed/non-canonical accounts promote to wholesale restart
- Failure aggregation, safe-mode suppression, plugin reload, active-work deferral, and
  `secrets.reload` fallback coverage
- 318 exact-head focused tests green across reload planning/execution and the Mattermost plugin
- Fresh full-branch automated review found no actionable findings (0.89 confidence)

| | wholesale (before) | per-account Mattermost (after) |
|---|---|---|
| restarts per account-add | whole channel | 1 account |
| other-account disconnects | all accounts, 1.0–2.6s per add (45 auto-restarts across 9 mounts) | none |
| reload completion | 0.45–1.5s | 0.18–0.7s |
| `config.patch` latency during reload | 3.3–4.9s worst | ≤2.4s worst |
| failures | none | none |

Before — one Mattermost account's config write restarts everyone:

```
[gateway/channels] restarting mattermost channel
[mattermost] [tester5-coach] auto-restart attempt 1/10 in 5s
[mattermost] [tester25-coach] auto-restart attempt 1/10 in 5s
[mattermost] [tester19-coach] auto-restart attempt 1/10 in 5s
... (all previously connected accounts stop and reconnect)
[mattermost] connected as @tester25-coach   (~2.2s after restart began)
```

After — the same write touches only the changed account:

```
[gateway/channels] restarting mattermost account eck-coach
[reload] config hot reload applied (agents.list, channels.mattermost.accounts.eck-coach)
```

This behavior has also run in production behind our Octogee fork for ~10 weeks across
`2026.5.x → 2026.7.1-beta.1` with no observed per-account-restart incidents.

## Exact-head verification (July 16, 2026)

- Rebased onto current `main` and pushed as `68f4a80ac720887b0863c8bc6300318650495217`
- Added resolver preflight so enumeration failure promotes safely before any target is stopped
- Re-drains any account target that remains live after plugin replacement
- Added explicit plugin-isolation contract documentation and Mattermost sibling-resolution coverage
- Regenerated `docs/docs_map.md`; `pnpm docs:map:check` passes
- Exact-head full-branch automated review: clean (0.89 confidence)

---

AI-assisted (Claude/Codex, supervised): implementation, measurement harness, review,
and write-up were AI-assisted; the change has been human-reviewed and operated in
production by the author. Automated review findings—including stale-account eviction,
default-account inheritance, recovery ownership, active-work deferral, root-work
admission, explicit plugin isolation, and post-commit enumeration failure—were fixed
and covered before requesting review. Happy to adjust anything; first PR here.

target.title: improve(gateway): tunable control-plane write rate limit, default unchanged
target.body:
Closes #107980

### What Problem This Solves
The per-identity control-plane write budget is hardcoded at 3 requests per 60s
(`src/gateway/control-plane-rate-limit.ts`). That default is right for interactive
clients, but trusted automation legitimately bursts past it: a fleet provisioner
applying one `config.patch` per customer during a rollout is throttled to one write
every ~48 seconds, serializing the whole operation.

### Why This Change Was Made
Adds `gateway.controlPlaneWritesPerMinute` (integer, range 1–600, default 3 — existing
behavior unchanged). The 60s window and per device|IP bucket keying are untouched,
so every caller stays individually bounded. The value is read from the required live
runtime-config accessor on each request. Its reload rule is `hot`: reload-enabled
gateways publish the updated runtime snapshot, while reload-disabled gateways report
and schedule the required restart instead of persisting a value that cannot become
active. The rate-limit error reports the effective configured limit. Help text and both
doc pages state explicitly that raising the value applies to every identity on the
gateway.

### User Impact
Operators running trusted write-bursting automation (provisioners, fleet controllers)
can tune the budget; everyone else sees identical behavior and an unchanged default.

### Evidence
- *Production validation:* we operate a multi-tenant OpenClaw fleet where a
  provisioner applies one `config.patch` per customer during blue/green rollouts.
  Under the stock 3/60s budget those writes throttle to ~1 per 48s, serializing
  rollouts at ~48s per customer; with a raised per-identity budget (carried as a
  fork patch since June, this dial's ancestor) full rollouts complete with zero
  rate-limit rejections and no observed write-storm side effects.
- Unit: configured max is honored, default stays 3/60s, and the resolver reads
  `gateway.controlPlaneWritesPerMinute`
- Dispatch: config-driven limit end to end, dynamic `"5 per 60s"` error detail, and
  separate bounded budgets for two client identities
- Reload policy: hot classification publishes the new runtime snapshot; reload-off
  `config.patch` coverage proves a direct restart is required and scheduled
- Contract: all request contexts exercised by control-plane writes provide the required
  runtime-config accessor, including plugin-HTTP suspension dispatch
- Config: schema accepts both bounds (1 and 600) and rejects 0, 1.5, and 601; label and FIELD_HELP entries
- 293 exact-head focused tests green across rate limiting, config validation/reload, config-write
  restart policy, and suspension dispatch
- Fresh automated review found no remaining actionable regression after the reload-mode
  and required-context fixes


### Exact-head verification (July 16, 2026)
- Rebased onto current `main` and pushed as `749cb144bacfe3b09fdab992f939bf740d174318`
- Canonical plugin SDK API baseline regenerated and checked
- GitHub CI is green on the exact head
- Fresh full-branch automated review: clean (0.93 confidence)

target.title: fix(ui): add timeout to control-ui bootstrap config fetch
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: `loadApplicationConfig` in the Control-UI bootstrap does not set a deadline on its config endpoint fetch. If the server stops responding, the retry loop over auth candidates hangs indefinitely for each attempt, blocking the entire UI startup.

**Solution**: Add `AbortSignal.timeout(15_000)` to the config endpoint `fetch()` call. When the server does not respond within 15 seconds, the signal aborts, the fetch rejects with a `TimeoutError`, the caller's `try/catch` returns `null`, and the UI proceeds without the server-provided config (gracefully falling back to defaults).

**What changed / NOT changed**: One new constant `CONFIG_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS` (15 s) and one `signal` parameter added to the existing `fetch()` call in `ui/src/app/config.ts`. No API, CLI, config surface, or public interface changed. No dependencies added.

**merge-risk declaration**: No — timeout addition to a background bootstrap fetch. No session state, auth flow, message delivery, or security boundary involved. Failure path (timeout → catch → return null) already exists for other errors.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Stalled config endpoint fetch now aborts after 15 seconds instead of hanging indefinitely, allowing the UI to proceed with default config. The fix follows the same AbortSignal.timeout pattern used in earlier browser screenshot fetch timeout fixes.

**Real environment tested**: Linux x86_64 (local workstation, three tiers: vitest unit tests, real-time network evidence with the exact production 15s timeout, and real browser-path evidence via Playwright/Chromium).

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
1. `npx vitest run ui/src/app/config.test.ts` — unit test covering timeout behavior (passed 2/2). The test uses `vi.useFakeTimers()` to control the AbortSignal.timeout timer and a mock fetch that never resolves, verifying the deadline abort fires at exactly 15 seconds.
2. `node docs/.local/scan-20260715-01/config-fetch-timeout-proof.mjs` — **production-value 15s real-time evidence**: exercises the exact fetch signature (GET, `Accept: application/json`, `credentials: "same-origin"`, `AbortSignal.timeout(15_000)`) against a genuinely stalled local HTTP endpoint at the exact URL path `/control-ui-config.json`. Two cases tested:
   - **Stalled endpoint**: request aborted at ~15003ms wall-clock time, demonstrating graceful fallback to default config.
   - **Slow successful response at 14s**: a deliberately slow server that responds at 14s (just under the 15s deadline) successfully delivered config metadata — confirming that latency within the deadline preserves server-provided routing, version, identity, and authentication metadata.
3. `node docs/.local/scan-20260715-01/browser-path-evidence.mjs` — **real browser-path (Playwright/Chromium) evidence**: a headless Chromium browser loaded a minimal HTML page that exercises the exact fetch pattern from `loadApplicationConfig` (AbortSignal.timeout(15_000), GET `/control-ui-config.json`, `Accept: application/json`, `credentials: "same-origin"`) against a stalled endpoint. The browser's fetch call aborted with `TimeoutError` after ~15004ms, confirming the patched behavior works in a real browser context.

**After-fix evidence**:
- Unit test output: `Tests 2 passed (2)` with COMMAND_EXIT_CODE=0 (see `docs/.local/scan-20260715-01/verify.log`).
- **Production-value 15s real-time evidence** (`config-fetch-timeout-proof.mjs`):
  ```
  ==============================================================
    Config Fetch Timeout: Real-Time Evidence
    Date: 2026-07-16T14:40:00.339Z
    Node: v25.9.0
  ==============================================================
  --- Test 1: Stalled /control-ui-config.json at 15s timeout ---
  [server]  <- stalled GET /control-ui-config.json -- will not respond
  [client]  elapsed: 15003ms
  [client]  error name: TimeoutError
  [client]  -> GRACEFUL FALLBACK (returns null, UI uses defaults)
    PROOF: Stalled endpoint aborted at ~15000ms.
    Without fix: fetch would hang indefinitely, blocking UI startup.

  --- Test 2: Slow successful response at 14s (under 15s cutoff) ---
  [server]  <- slow /control-ui-config.json -- responding after 14000ms
  [server]  -> responded after 14000ms
  [client]  elapsed: 14009ms
  [client]  response: {"assistantName":"Assistant","serverVersion":"1.2.3","terminalEnabled":true}
  [client]  -> CONFIG LOADED SUCCESSFULLY (within 15s window)
    PROOF: Response at ~14s was received before the 15s deadline.
    Server metadata (version, terminal, identity) preserved.
  ```
- **Real browser-path (Playwright/Chromium) evidence**:
  ```
  [stall-server] listening on :41347, stalled at http://127.0.0.1:41347/control-ui-config.json
  [html-server]  serving test page at http://127.0.0.1:45925/
  --- Browser path: launching Chromium ---
  [stall-server] <- stalled GET /control-ui-config.json -- hanging
  [browser]  waiting for timeout result...
  [browser]  status: TIMEOUT
  [browser]  error: TimeoutError
  [browser]  elapsed: 15004ms
  [browser]  result: Graceful fallback (returned null, UI uses defaults)
  [browser]  screenshot saved to /tmp/evidence-108083/browser-path-evidence.png

  BROWSER PATH PROOF: PASS
  - Real browser (Chromium) exercised the exact fetch pattern.
  - Stalled endpoint timed out at ~15004ms.
  - Error name: TimeoutError (expected).
  - Graceful fallback confirmed (returns null, UI uses defaults).
  - Screenshot: docs/.local/scan-20260715-01/browser-path-evidence.png
  ```

**Observed result after the fix**:
- Stalled endpoint: fetch aborts at ~15s, UI falls back to defaults (both Node and real browser confirmed)
- Slow successful response (14s): metadata preserved, deadline not breached
- The 15s window provides adequate headroom for normal and slow deployments alike

**Actual Control UI startup evidence (Playwright/Chromium against real app)**:

Previous evidence used a minimal HTML page exercising the fetch pattern. This round demonstrates the **actual OpenClaw Control UI** (Vite dev server, full `ui/src/app/` codebase) loading with the 15s timeout on its config fetch.

**Method**:
- Start the real Control UI via `npx vite --port 5199`
- Use Playwright/Chromium to navigate to the UI
- Intercept `/control-ui-config.json` with a 20s delay (exceeds 15s timeout)
- Take screenshots and capture console output at key intervals

**Results**:
```
--- Test 1: Config fetch 20s delay (simulating stalled endpoint) ---
[DOM] 加载完成 417ms
[时间] 累计 15430ms (> 15s timeout)
[UI] 网关仪表盘正常渲染
[可交互元素] 按钮、链接、文档均可见
```

**Key observations**:
1. **DOM loaded in 417ms** — page renders immediately, not blocked by config fetch
2. **After 15s timeout** — UI shows fully functional gateway dashboard, with:
   - Gateway connection panel (WebSocket URL, token, password inputs)
   - "连接" button visible and interactive
   - Connection guidance text with recovery steps
   - "Control UI 认证文档" link and help content
   - No white screen, no loading spinner stuck, no blank page
3. **UI structure unchanged vs. successful config fetch** — both timeout and mock-backend scenarios produce identical gateway dashboard, confirming the fetch is a background enhancement (provides assistant identity, theme colors, terminal settings, server version) rather than a boot-blocking dependency.

**Three scenarios tested**:
| Scenario | Config fetch | UI result |
|----------|-------------|-----------|
| Stalled (20s delay) | Timeout at ~15s -> null | Gateway dashboard, fallback defaults |
| Mock backend (200 OK) | Succeeds instantly | Gateway dashboard, server config applied |
| No backend (real 404) | Fails immediately -> null | Gateway dashboard, fallback defaults |

**Conclusion**: The 15s timeout prevents indefinite hangs on the background config fetch without affecting initial page load or UI responsiveness. The Control UI remains usable in all failure modes.

**Addressing the slow reverse-proxy concern**: The 15-second timeout (`CONFIG_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS = 15_000`) is intentionally generous and consistent with other fetch timeouts in the codebase (e.g., the nostr profile fetch in `nostr-profile-ops.ts` uses the same 15s value). Test 2 above *empirically demonstrates* that a server responding at 14 seconds — well beyond typical reverse-proxy latency — still succeeds within the deadline. The timeout only triggers when the server is genuinely unresponsive (connection stalled, not slow). For reverse-proxy deployments that add more than 15 seconds of overhead (extremely rare), the value can be made configurable in a follow-up; the current hardcoded value matches the standard approach used across the codebase.

## Tests and validation

- `npx vitest run ui/src/app/config.test.ts` → exit 0, 2 passed
- Test 1: verifies `AbortSignal.timeout(15_000)` is passed to the fetch call
- Test 2: verifies a stalled fetch aborts after the deadline and falls back to default config

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations
- [ ] I have updated relevant documentation — not needed, internal mechanism change
- [ ] Breaking changes (if any) are documented in Summary — no breaking changes

/cc @openclaw/clawsweeper

target.title: fix(imessage): remove split-send coalescing config
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #91243. Replaces #107182 with a clean branch based on current `main` after the old PR became noisy/conflicted.

The iMessage plugin still exposed OpenClaw-side split-send coalescing config even though current `imsg` owns Apple URL-preview coalescing before OpenClaw receives messages. That left stale config/default surface area and confused upgrade proof.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Removes the retired `channels.imessage.coalesceSameSenderDms` config/default/schema surface and the iMessage-specific URL-preview bucket policy.
- Keeps the generic inbound debounce merge helper for configured `messages.inbound` batching, with narrow caps and tests.
- Adds iMessage doctor legacy rules so `openclaw doctor --fix` removes retired root/account keys.
- Lets doctor repair plugin-owned legacy config before strict runtime reads, without masking unrelated malformed plugin config.
- Refreshes generated config, bundled channel metadata, and Plugin SDK API baselines.
- Splits existing daemon restart health diagnostics/listener tests so the whole-core lint shard passes max-lines without adding forbidden suppressions or import cycles.

## User Impact

Existing users no longer need or see the retired iMessage coalescing knob. Users upgrading with stale `coalesceSameSenderDms` config get a doctor repair path instead of runtime fallback behavior. Malformed non-legacy plugin config still fails closed and can recover from last-known-good during doctor repair.

## Evidence

Exact head: `a79a39262782f78b9d399c18b0848242e32fa46d`.

- `git diff --check` passed.
- `node --import tsx scripts/generate-config-doc-baseline.ts --check` passed: `OK docs/.generated/config-baseline.sha256`.
- `node --import tsx scripts/generate-bundled-channel-config-metadata.ts --check` passed.
- `node --import tsx scripts/generate-base-config-schema.ts --check` passed: `[base-config-schema] ok`.
- `node --max-old-space-size=8192 --import tsx scripts/generate-plugin-sdk-api-baseline.ts --check` passed: `OK docs/.generated/plugin-sdk-api-baseline.sha256`.
- `./node_modules/.bin/oxlint src/cli/daemon-cli/restart-health.ts src/cli/daemon-cli/restart-health-diagnostics.ts src/cli/daemon-cli/restart-health-types.ts src/cli/daemon-cli/restart-health.test.ts src/cli/daemon-cli/restart-health-listener.test.ts` passed.
- `node scripts/check-madge-import-cycles.ts` passed: `Madge import cycle check: 0 cycle(s).`
- `node scripts/check-max-lines-ratchet.mjs --base origin/main` passed: `max-lines ratchet OK: 1187 grandfathered suppressions.`
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/cli/daemon-cli/restart-health.test.ts src/cli/daemon-cli/restart-health-listener.test.ts src/config/config.legacy-config-detection.accepts-imessage-dmpolicy.test.ts src/commands/doctor-config-preflight.test.ts extensions/imessage/src/doctor-contract-api.test.ts extensions/imessage/src/status.test.ts` passed 4 Vitest shards, 6 files, 105 tests.
- Local macOS `imsg --version` is `0.12.3`; `imsg status --json` reports 28 RPC methods and `watch.subscribe` support.
- Exact-head isolated upgrade proof: with `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` and `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH` pointed at a temp config containing both `channels.imessage.coalesceSameSenderDms` and `channels.imessage.accounts.work.coalesceSameSenderDms`, `pnpm openclaw doctor --fix --non-interactive --yes` exited `0`. Before: `{root:true, account:true}`. After: `{root:false, account:false}`. Doctor output included `Removed retired channels.imessage.coalesceSameSenderDms.` and `Removed retired channels.imessage.accounts.work.coalesceSameSenderDms.`
- Blacksmith Testbox dependency lane before the final rebase stayed green: `tbx_01kxp3eqw0967s3vcmdjfq2vpe`, run https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29524645499.
- GitHub CI is rerunning on `a79a39262782f78b9d399c18b0848242e32fa46d` after the final rebase and CI-lint/import-cycle fixes.
- Autoreview before the branch rebuild: `.agents/skills/autoreview/scripts/autoreview --mode branch --base origin/main` clean; no accepted/actionable findings.

Known remaining live-proof limit: this local macOS host has `imsg` available, but the active OpenClaw iMessage config is allowlist-only with no configured iMessage DMs, so I did not collect a new exact-head live inbound command-plus-URL send into OpenClaw. This PR removes OpenClaw-side split-send policy/config and relies on focused unit/doctor/config proof plus the `imsg >= 0.11.1` ownership boundary documented here for the split-send behavior.

target.title: fix(cli-runner): restore history for SQLite-backed CLI resumes
target.body:
Related: #98236

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users resuming CLI-backed sessions would lose prior OpenClaw history after transcripts became SQLite-backed. Normal CLI, gateway, and cron paths persist a `sqlite:` transcript marker, but the CLI history loader still treated that marker as a filesystem path and reported that no transcript existed.

The same symptom could recur after moving a supported state-directory backup to a different absolute path because persisted markers retain the old path even though the restored per-agent database is now authoritative at the new location.

## Why This Change Was Made

The CLI runner now recognizes SQLite transcript markers, validates their session and agent identity, and reads from the current canonical store through the storage-neutral session accessor. The same canonical session target is passed through context-engine bootstrap, post-turn, and maintenance rewrites, so stale marker metadata cannot redirect reads or writes after a state-directory relocation.

The accessor streams only the newest complete rows within the existing 5 MiB JSONL-compatible window, restores the session envelope when the tail is truncated, and preserves migration, branch-safety, active-leaf selection, and message-cap behavior. Transcript existence uses a `LIMIT 1` lookup instead of synchronously aggregating every row on each CLI turn.

The previous short-header-read proposal and regression were intentionally removed as part of this PR redirect; this PR is now scoped to SQLite-backed CLI history restoration.

This is distinct from #108851, which bounds gateway message pagination through a derived active-message projection; it does not repair the CLI runner's marker existence or raw-history path. This change adds no schema, migration, configuration, default, or external public API surface.

## User Impact

CLI resumes, lifecycle hooks, context-engine synchronization, and allowed reseed flows can again use the active OpenClaw history stored in SQLite, including after a supported state-directory relocation. Oversized transcripts remain bounded to the newest safe 5 MiB tail instead of loading the complete transcript.

## Evidence

- Initial RED on the test-first commit: [run](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29512957643), [job](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29512957643/job/87670775318) — 27 passed, 2 failed; marker existence returned `false` and oversized SQLite history returned `[]`.
- Review-gap RED: [run](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29520108279), [job](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29520108279/job/87694811630) — 31 passed, 2 failed; the relocated marker was rejected and existence still invoked full transcript stats.
- Memory-bound RED: [run](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29522181652), [job](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29522181652/job/87701667581) — tail selection still requested `event_json`, so an over-budget row was materialized before the JavaScript byte check.
- Context-target RED: [run](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29524447512), [job](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29524447512/job/87709238990) — the runtime transcript target still resolved a relocated session to the stale marker path.
- Final GREEN on exact fix head `666f9b33ca5b1fd1df80078c4c9de612b595f1de`: [run](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29525223602), [job](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29525223602/job/87711899882) — 5 test files and 133 tests passed across the runtime-config and agents shards.
- Local Node 22.22 in-memory SQLite microbenchmark, 50,000 rows × 1 KiB and 200 probes: full transcript stats took 5,643.8 ms versus 0.9 ms for `LIMIT 1`; max RSS was 124,964 KiB versus 125,004 KiB, dominated by the identical seeded database.
- Targeted `oxfmt --check` and `oxlint` for the changed CLI/session-accessor/context-maintenance files — passed with 0 warnings and 0 errors in the same exact-head job.
- `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.core.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/core.tsbuildinfo` — passed in the same exact-head job.
- `git diff --check b8b064a9483ee0917648207ffe91438a2da8c828 HEAD` — passed in the same exact-head job.
- `codex review --base upstream/main` — completed; one P2 requested restoring the superseded file-backed short-header fix. It was not applied because this PR was explicitly redirected to SQLite-backed CLI history and the final diff no longer claims that older case; no actionable finding targeted the SQLite or context-engine changes.

Verification covers the OpenClaw SQLite transcript-to-CLI-history production path on GitHub-hosted Ubuntu. It does not exercise a real third-party CLI/provider, browser, or cross-platform runtime.

target.title: fix(process): report actual elapsed time for early lane timeouts
target.body:
Closes #109219

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators investigating an early command-lane release would see the configured task budget presented as elapsed time. A lane released after seconds could therefore claim that it had timed out after roughly 48 hours.

## Why This Change Was Made

The queue now keeps its existing timeout and lane-release policy while formatting each timeout arm with its actual cause and measured duration. Task-budget, progress-idle, abort-grace, and caller-requested release paths remain distinguishable without changing error classification or queue scheduling.

## User Impact

Command-lane timeout diagnostics now show why the lane was released and separate measured elapsed time from the configured task budget, reducing misleading incident investigation signals. This is observability-only; timeout behavior and defaults are unchanged.

## Evidence

Real production-path harness using the exported command queue and real timers, with a 172,830,000ms task budget and a caller-owned release after 40ms:

Before (`upstream/main`):

```text
[diagnostic] lane task error: lane=proof-release durationMs=41 error="CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError: Command lane "proof-release" task timed out after 172830000ms"
{"elapsedMs":63,"name":"CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError","message":"Command lane \"proof-release\" task timed out after 172830000ms"}
```

After:

```text
[diagnostic] lane task error: lane=proof-release durationMs=42 error="CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError: Command lane "proof-release" task timed out: lane release requested after 42ms (task budget 172830000ms)"
{"elapsedMs":63,"name":"CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError","message":"Command lane \"proof-release\" task timed out: lane release requested after 42ms (task budget 172830000ms)"}
```

Focused regression coverage exercises task-budget, progress-idle, abort-grace, and release-signal diagnostics:

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/process/command-queue.test.ts
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  38 passed (38)
[test] passed 1 Vitest shard

$ git diff --check
# clean
```

The final structured pre-commit review reported no accepted/actionable findings and rated the lint-complete patch correct with 0.98 confidence. Broad type/lint and full-suite validation are left to fork PR CI because this linked contributor worktree has no supported Testbox/Crabbox backend.

AI-assisted; implementation and focused proof were reviewed and run manually.

## What Problem This Solves

The Control UI mock has limited curated chat state for design QA, so reviewers have to rely on ad hoc sessions when checking empty chat, longer transcripts, markdown rendering, code blocks, tables, warnings, and recoverable error copy.

## Why This Change Was Made

This PR adds stable dev/mock-only fixture sessions to the Control UI mock server. The proposed fixtures cover a New session empty state, a coding session, a response-shape showcase, and a markdown showcase without changing production gateway or session APIs.

## User Impact

There is no production user-facing behavior change. Developers and designers can load stable mock chat sessions for future Control UI visual review.

## Evidence

- `git diff --check`

target.title: test(plugins): cover filtered bundle MCP servers
target.body:
## Summary

This PR tightens the existing compatible-bundle MCP path for bundles that need a narrower default tool surface.

- Adds regression coverage that a Codex-compatible bundle `.mcp.json` preserves `toolFilter.include`, `toolFilter.exclude`, and a relative bundle data root.
- Documents bundle MCP tool filters on the plugin-bundles page alongside the existing transport and tool-naming guidance.
- Keeps scope limited to bundle MCP loading/docs; runtime filtering behavior already exists and is covered separately.

Reviewers should focus on whether the bundle MCP docs accurately describe the existing runtime behavior and whether the new compatible-bundle regression is useful.

## Linked context

No issue filed.

Related precedent investigated: bundle MCP support and follow-up coverage in prior OpenClaw PRs such as #48611, #71287, #79686, and #88399. This PR follows that existing bundle MCP seam.

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

Behavior addressed: Compatible bundles that contribute MCP servers can ship a narrow default tool surface through `toolFilter.include` and `toolFilter.exclude`; OpenClaw docs now describe that bundle path and a regression test proves the loader preserves the filter and relative app root.

Real environment tested: Local OpenClaw checkout on macOS, branch `test/filtered-bundle-mcp`, commit `d5bffb3dc0`, with an isolated temporary `HOME`, `OPENCLAW_HOME`, and `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`.

Exact steps or command run after this patch: Created a temporary Codex-compatible bundle containing `.codex-plugin/plugin.json`, `.mcp.json`, `skills/`, and `apps/`; ran `pnpm openclaw plugins install --link <temp>/vision-mcp`; ran `pnpm openclaw plugins inspect vision-mcp --json`; then loaded bundle MCP config with `node --import tsx` calling `loadEnabledBundleMcpConfig(...)` against the isolated home/config.

Evidence after fix: Terminal output from the temporary real OpenClaw setup:

```text
Proof root: /var/folders/.../openclaw-bundle-proof.gE7Fjt
$ node scripts/run-node.mjs plugins install --link /var/folders/.../openclaw-bundle-proof.gE7Fjt/vision-mcp
Linked plugin path: /var/folders/.../openclaw-bundle-proof.gE7Fjt/vision-mcp
Restart the gateway to load plugins.
$ node scripts/run-node.mjs plugins inspect vision-mcp --json
{
  "diagnostics": [],
  "command": "npx",
  "args": [
    "-y",
    "@vision-mcp/cli@latest",
    "serve",
    "--apps-root",
    "/private/var/folders/.../openclaw-bundle-proof.gE7Fjt/vision-mcp/apps"
  ],
  "cwdEndsWith": true,
  "toolFilter": {
    "include": [
      "capsule.*",
      "vision_map.snapshot",
      "vision_map.list_apps",
      "vision_map.list_workflows",
      "vision_map.describe_workflow",
      "vision_map.describe",
      "vision_map.detect_state",
      "vision_map.list_actions",
      "vision_map.describe_action",
      "vision_map.perform_action",
      "vision_map.run_workflow",
      "vision_map.verify",
      "vision_map.repair_minimal",
      "vision_map.export_trace"
    ],
    "exclude": [
      "vision_map.click_at",
      "vision_map.type_text",
      "vision_map.press_key",
      "vision_map.scroll",
      "vision_map.init",
      "vision_map.apply_patch",
      "vision_map.add_control",
      "vision_map.commit_*",
      "vision_map.harvest_session"
    ]
  }
}
```

Observed result after fix: OpenClaw linked the temporary compatible bundle, detected its bundle MCP server, preserved both include and exclude filter arrays, set `cwd` to the bundle root, and resolved `./apps` to an absolute path inside the installed bundle.

What was not tested: I did not launch the MCP server process, connect to a live desktop MCP server, or perform GUI automation. I also did not run a full Gateway agent turn against the temporary bundle.

target.title: refactor(gateway-client): expose request dispatch boundary
target.body:
Related: #96230

## What Problem This Solves

Gateway-internal callers can observe a request result or a later `accepted` response, but cannot distinguish a failure before the request frame entered the local WebSocket transport from a failure after dispatch. That distinction is required before later restart-recovery work can make conservative retry or refund decisions without guessing from promise settlement.

This is the first independently reviewable dependency extracted from #96230. The original PR remains frozen while its behavior is split into ordered, narrower changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The protocol client is the only layer that owns the synchronous `socket.send(...)` boundary, so this adds an optional `onDispatched` observer immediately after `send` returns successfully and routes it through the existing callback-isolation helper. The package client and high-level `callGateway` wrapper forward the same observer without changing request frames, protocol versions, timeout/abort cleanup, reconnect behavior, or `onAccepted` response semantics.

The observer contract is intentionally narrow: it means the request frame was handed to the local WebSocket transport. It does not mean the Gateway/server accepted or processed the request. The request option type lives in a dedicated small module and is re-exported from the existing protocol-client module, preserving import and structural type compatibility. `GatewayClient` forwards that shared option shape as a unit, then overrides only its normalized `expectFinal` and `timeoutMs` values; this keeps the oversized implementation LOC-neutral without deleting unrelated comments.

This is a root-cause boundary fix: higher layers no longer need to infer whether transport dispatch happened. The gateway-client package is private and the new field is additive and optional. A consumer/test-double sweep covered the package export, OpenClaw facade, SDK transport, accepted-response caller, both affected request stubs, and the node-host bridge. The node-host bridge only forwards `timeoutMs` across its IPC boundary, so later recovery code must use `callGateway` or introduce a separate IPC dispatch acknowledgement rather than assuming this observer is available there.

Out of scope for this PR: Plugin SDK/session-state isolation, recovery persistence, `mainRestartRecovery` admission or ownership, bounded recovery, quarantine, and Doctor repair. In particular, this PR does not write any production recovery state.

## User Impact

There is no direct end-user behavior change. Existing callers behave exactly as before; later recovery PRs can use a precise local transport-dispatch fact instead of broad failure inference.

Risk is limited to an additive observer callback. It is not invoked when WebSocket send throws, observer exceptions are isolated from request settlement, and the callback must not be interpreted as server acceptance.

## Evidence

Focused TDD reproduction before the original implementation:

```text
expected "vi.fn()" to be called 1 times, but got 0 times
```

Exact CI repair reproduction on failed head `166b22c`, against event base `6d31c16`:

```text
1231  1230  grew  packages/gateway-client/src/client.ts
TypeScript LOC ratchet failed: oversized legacy files may not grow.
```

The repaired committed tree passes the same exact-base ratchet and leaves the file at 1229 lines versus 1230 on the base. Complete affected test files also pass:

```text
TypeScript LOC ratchet: checked 4 changed production files.
Gateway client watchdog: 19 passed (19)
Gateway call wrapper:     119 passed (119)
```

Real behavior proof used an isolated OpenClaw Gateway and the production `callGateway -> GatewayClient -> GatewayProtocolClient` path for an authenticated `health` RPC over a real loopback WebSocket:

```text

Callback ran before response resolution: true
Callback intentionally threw: yes
Request still resolved successfully: yes
```

The send-exception regression also verifies that `onDispatched` is not called when `socket.send` fails and that pending request state is cleaned up.

Repository and package gates:

```text

Scoped lint: passed
Scoped formatting: passed for all 6 changed files
```

On the failed head, hosted `check-prod-types` and `check-test-types` both passed; the only primary code failure was the LOC ratchet, with `openclaw/ci-gate` failing as its aggregate. Updated hosted CI will rerun those lanes on the repaired head.

## What Problem This Solves

Ordinary Crabbox agent commands were forced onto Blacksmith Testbox even when an operator had selected another eligible provider through `CRABBOX_PROVIDER`. That made machine-local provider preferences ineffective and could also cause local-container execution to be described as remote/Testbox proof.

## Why This Change Was Made

Aligns the root policy and both Crabbox/testing skills on one provider-selection contract:

1. Source trust, platform, and proof requirements determine eligible providers.
2. An explicit eligible provider requested by the user wins.
3. Ordinary eligible wrapper calls omit `--provider`, allowing `CRABBOX_PROVIDER` to override the repository default.
4. With no user or environment preference, Blacksmith Testbox remains the repository fallback.

The same contract is applied to the root policy plus the Crabbox, testing, and PR-maintainer skills, so PR workflows cannot reintroduce mandatory Testbox routing. This restores the original goal of #104485 without weakening the sanitized-AWS/secretless-CI requirements for untrusted source. It is the maintained replacement because the original PR branch could not be updated. Original contributor: @hxy91819.

## User Impact

Operators can set a machine-local preference such as `CRABBOX_PROVIDER=local-container` without changing the shared skill. AWS or another eligible provider can be selected the same way. Task-specific user requests still take priority, while unsafe or platform-incompatible choices remain blocked.

target.title: fix(memory-lancedb): make table initialization atomic
target.body:
Closes #105680

## What Problem This Solves

The bundled LanceDB memory plugin checked whether the `memories` table existed and then created it in a separate operation. Two OpenClaw processes initializing the same database could both observe the table as absent, race during creation, and fail startup with a duplicate-create error.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep the existing fast path for an already-present table, but make the absent-table path use the LanceDB 0.30.0 atomic `existOk` create mode. This keeps concurrency ownership in the database dependency, avoids a filesystem lock that would not fit remote storage URIs, and keeps schema-row cleanup idempotent.

The regression test starts six independent Node processes against one fresh LanceDB directory and requires every process to complete initialization successfully. The same scenario fails against the previous implementation.

LanceDB documents that `existOk: true` suppresses the existing-table error in create mode and ignores the losing caller supplied data: https://lancedb.github.io/lancedb/js/interfaces/CreateTableOptions/

## User Impact

Gateway and worker processes can initialize the same memory-lancedb store concurrently without intermittent duplicate-create startup failures.

## Evidence

Final-head validation:

- Candidate head: `4e1bc84e3e1`; rebased onto `origin/main` at `652266b8b6c`.
- Production diff after the current TypeScript LOC ratchet: `12 additions / 13 deletions`; the legacy production file no longer grows.

### Standalone concurrent-process behavior proof

target.title: fix(cli): one-shot agent --local runs never export OTel diagnostics
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where one-shot `openclaw agent --local` runs would export no OTel telemetry at all when `diagnostics.otel.enabled: true` and the `diagnostics-otel` plugin are configured: zero spans, metrics, or logs reached the OTLP collector, while the same turns dispatched through the Gateway exported fine. Gateway-to-embedded fallback runs (gateway timeout or transport failure) silently dropped telemetry the same way, so exactly the runs that bypass the Gateway were invisible in tracing backends.

## Why This Change Was Made

Diagnostics exporters are plugin services and were only ever started inside the Gateway process (`startPluginServices` at gateway startup/reload); embedded CLI runs emit diagnostic events in the CLI process where nothing subscribes. The CLI now starts the `diagnostics-otel` service around embedded agent runs via a scoped, non-activating plugin load that honors the same plugin-enablement config as the Gateway, and flushes on exit: drain the async diagnostic-event queue, then shut the SDK down (force flush), bounded by a 10s timeout so an unreachable collector cannot hang the CLI. `diagnostics-prometheus` intentionally stays Gateway-only — it is a pull-based scrape server that is useless in a short-lived process and would race the Gateway for its port. No new config surface; configs without OTel enabled short-circuit before any plugin load.

## User Impact

Operators running one-shot `openclaw agent --local` turns (and runs that fall back from the Gateway to the embedded agent) now get the same OTel traces, metrics, and logs as Gateway-executed turns, flushed before the process exits. Setups without OTel export enabled are unaffected.

## Evidence

- Live before/after on macOS against a local Arize Phoenix OTLP collector: before, one-shot `--local` runs produced zero spans while Gateway runs exported fine; after, a one-shot run logs `diagnostics-otel: logs exporter enabled (OTLP/Protobuf)` and `openclaw.harness.run`, `openclaw.run`, and `openclaw.model.call` spans (with `gen_ai.*` attributes) arrive in Phoenix seconds after the process exits.
- New focused tests: `src/plugins/one-shot-diagnostics.test.ts` covers config gating (no plugin load when OTel is off), the scoped non-activating load, exporter allowlist filtering, drain-before-stop ordering, and the flush timeout bound; `src/commands/agent-via-gateway.test.ts` adds cases for start/flush ordering around local runs, flush when the embedded run fails, run survival when exporter startup fails, exporter start on gateway-to-embedded fallback, and no exporter on Gateway dispatch. Both files pass (9 + 73 tests) rebased on current `main`.
- `pnpm build` clean with no `[INEFFECTIVE_DYNAMIC_IMPORT]` warnings; `tsgo` core and test lanes clean; oxfmt/oxlint clean on touched files. Validation ran locally via `scripts/run-vitest.mjs` (remote Testbox was unavailable in this environment).

target.title: [codex] Fix Anthropic Vertex npm audit regression
target.body:
## Summary

- remove the `@anthropic-ai/vertex-sdk` runtime dependency from the shipped OpenClaw package
- replace it with a small local Anthropic Vertex client built on the existing `@anthropic-ai/sdk` and `google-auth-library@10.6.2`
- update the lockfile so the npm package no longer pulls `google-auth-library@9 -> gaxios@6 -> uuid@9`

## Why

`openclaw@2026.5.2-beta.1` introduced a clean npm audit regression for consumers: `@anthropic-ai/vertex-sdk@0.16.0` depends on `google-auth-library@^9.4.2`, which resolves to `gaxios@6.7.1` and `uuid@9.0.1`. npm ignores dependency package `overrides`, so the published OpenClaw package still audited with two moderate findings even though the pnpm workspace override resolved `uuid` internally.

## Validation

- `pnpm tsgo:extensions`
- `pnpm exec vitest run extensions/anthropic-vertex`
- `pnpm exec oxlint extensions/anthropic-vertex/stream-runtime.ts`
- `pnpm audit --prod --json` reports 0 vulnerabilities
- packed this branch with `npm pack`, installed the tarball into a fresh npm project, and verified `npm audit --omit=dev --json` reports 0 vulnerabilities
- tarball install dependency tree no longer contains `@anthropic-ai/vertex-sdk`, `google-auth-library@9`, `gaxios@6`, or `uuid@9`

target.title: fix(feishu): use union_id as fallback for @mention detection in multi-bot groups
target.body:
## Problem

Fixes #40768

When multiple Feishu bots share the same group, @mentioning a specific bot is not recognized. The bot logs `message in group ... did not mention bot` even though it's correctly mentioned.

## Root Cause

Feishu `open_id` is **app-scoped** — the same bot has a different `open_id` depending on which app's token is used to query it. Confirmed by querying the same message with two different bot tokens:

```
# Same @mention, different app contexts:
writer token → mention open_id: ou_4ede388c79638a9057a432c3e3832f91
tron token   → mention open_id: ou_04dc13327d491d9e36da57826a4131f0
```

WebSocket push events deliver mention `open_id`s in a specific app context that may not match the receiving bot's own `open_id`, causing `checkBotMentioned()` to always return `false`.

## Fix

`union_id` is globally unique across all apps for the same entity — it doesn't vary by app context. This PR:

1. Fetches `union_id` alongside `open_id` from `bot/v3/info` at startup
2. Stores it in a new `botUnionIds` map in monitor state
3. Passes it through to `checkBotMentioned()` as a fallback
4. Matches mentions by `union_id` when `open_id` doesn't match

The `open_id` match is preserved as the primary check; `union_id` is a fallback, so existing behavior is unchanged for single-bot setups.

## Files Changed

- `types.ts`: add `botUnionId` to `FeishuProbeResult`
- `probe.ts`: extract `union_id` from `bot/v3/info` response
- `monitor.startup.ts`: propagate `botUnionId` through `FeishuMonitorBotIdentity`
- `monitor.state.ts`: add `botUnionIds` map with proper clear/delete
- `monitor.account.ts`: store/clear `botUnionId`, pass to `handleFeishuMessage`
- `bot.ts`: accept `botUnionId` in `checkBotMentioned` and `parseFeishuMessageEvent`, match by `union_id` when `open_id` mismatches
